Sūtradhāra:

Here I am; by the force of my role, I have become an inhabitant of Ayodhyā belonging to that time. (Looking all around) Ho there! While this is the time of the consecration of the venerable Rāma—the great king who was a comet to the clan of Paulastya—a time of uninterrupted festive music day and night—why then are the public squares devoid of wandering bards? (Entering) Actor: [Continues]...

Sir! Indeed, the high-souled monkeys and Rākṣasas who fought in the battle of Laṅkā, as well as the Brahman-sages and royal sages who sanctify various regions and attend upon the assembly, have been sent from their own homes by the Great King; it was for the sake of propitiating them that there has been such joy for so many days.
Sūtradhāra:
Ah, this is indeed the reason.
Actor:
Furthermore—
the queens, the mothers of Rāma, have departed under the protection of Vasiṣṭha.
Placing Arundhatī at their head, they went to the hermitage of their son-in-law for the sacrifice. ||3||
Sūtradhāra:
Since I am a stranger, I ask you: who, then, is the son-in-law? Naṭa: [He replies.]
King Daśaratha begot a daughter named Śāntā;
he gave her to King Romapāda as a foster-child.

The son of Vibhāṇḍaka, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, married her. He commenced a twelve-year sacrificial session (*satra*). Out of deference to him, the elders departed for that place, leaving Jānakī even though she was far advanced in pregnancy.
The Stage Manager:
So, what is the use of this? Come, let us go to the palace gate itself and attend upon it according to the custom of our own caste.
Actor:
Therefore, let the worthy one examine the King’s perfectly refined sequence of hymns for his attendance. Director:
O noble sir! One must always engage in worldly discourse; for how can there be immunity from censure?
Just as with women, so it is with words: people are quick to find fault even in excellence.
Actor: One must say he is an exceedingly wicked man;
for even Queen Vaidehī has been subjected to public censure because of him.
The root cause is residing in the house of a Rākṣasa, while there is uncertainty regarding purification by fire.
Sūtradhāra:
But if this rumor were to reach the Great King, then it would be a grievous matter.
Naṭa: [Agreeing]...
"In every way, the sages and the gods will provide for our welfare. (Walking about) "Ho there! Where is the great king now? (Listening) "Thus the people say:
'Having come out of affection to welcome him and having spent these days in celebration, Janaka has today departed for Videha.
Therefore, to console the queen who is despondent, the lord of men leaves the seat of justice and enters his private quarters. (7)
(Thus they both exit. This concludes the prologue. (Then enter Rāma and Sītā, seated.
Rāma:
O Queen, Vaidehī! Have confidence; for those elders of ours are unable to abandon us.
However, the necessity of performing [ritual] duties detracts from one's independence;
for the state of a householder who has established the sacred fires is fraught with difficulties due to the transgressions [that may occur]. (8)
Sītā:
I know it, noble husband! I know it. But the separation from one's kin is a cause of great anguish. Rāvaṇa:
It is so. For these are the conditions of saṃsāra that cut through the vitals of compassion; loathing them, the wise, having renounced all desires, find rest in the forest. (Entering) Chamberlain:
"Rāmabhadra! (leaving the sentence half-uttered, with apprehension) "Great King!"

Rāma: (Smiling) Noble sir! Indeed, the formal address "O Rāmabhadra! is most appropriate for one belonging to my father's retinue. Therefore, let me be addressed by whatever name you are accustomed to using. Chamberlain: [He speaks accordingly.]
"Your Majesty! Aṣṭāvakra has arrived from the hermitage of Ṛśyaśṛṅga.
Sītā: "Noble sir! Why, then, do you delay?"
Rāma:— Bring him in quickly. (The chamberlain exits. Entering) Aṣṭāvakra:—
"May it be well with you both.
Rāma:
"O Blessed One! I salute you; please be seated here."
Sītā:
Blessed one, salutations to you! Is all well with the elders, together with their son-in-law, and with the noble Śāntā?
Rāma: [Listens.]
"Is my venerable brother-in-law, the illustrious Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, free from obstacles and drinking the Soma juice, and is the noble Śāntā well?
Sītā said: "Does he remember us as well? (asmān api smarati?)
Aṣṭāvakra:—(Sitting down) Indeed so. O Queen! The venerable Vasiṣṭha, the family preceptor, says this to you:
"The divine Earth gave birth to you; King Janaka, equal to Prajāpati, is your father."
O daughter, you are the bride of those kings in whose lineages both the Sun-god and we ourselves are gurus. (9)
Therefore, what else can we hope for? Only this: may you give birth to a hero.
Rāma:
We are favored.
For in the case of worldly virtuous people, speech follows the meaning;
but in the case of the primordial seers (ṛṣis), the meaning runs after their speech.
Aṣṭāvakra:
Furthermore, the venerable Arundhatī, the queens, and Śāntā have repeatedly instructed me: "Whatever pregnancy-longing she may have must necessarily be honored by her without delay.
Rāma: [Listens.]
If she says this, [then] Aṣṭāvakra says:

"The sister-in-law and the Queen have sent word: 'Child, you were not brought here because your pregnancy was advanced. Prince Rāmabhadra, too, has been kept here solely for your diversion. Therefore, we shall see you, long-lived one, with your lap full of sons.'"
Rāma—(With a smile of joy and bashfulness) So be it. I have not been given any instruction by the venerable Vasiṣṭha. Aṣṭāvakra—
Listen!
We have been detained by the sacrifice for our son-in-law; you are but a child and your kingdom is new.
You ought to be intent upon pleasing your subjects, for fame is your supreme wealth. (11)
Rāma:
As the venerable son of Mitrāvaruṇa commands.
Whether it be affection, compassion, happiness, or even Jānaki herself—
For the sake of winning over the world, there is no pain for me in renouncing it. || 12 ||
Sītā:
That is precisely why my noble husband is the upholder of the Rāghava lineage.
Rāma: [Listens.]
"Who is there? Who is here, sir? Let Aṣṭāvakra rest.
Aṣṭāvakra—(Rising and walking about): Ah, Prince Lakṣmaṇa has arrived! (He exits. (Entering:)

Victory, victory to our noble lord! Noble brother, the painter Arjuna has depicted your life story on this wall exactly as we instructed him. May your noble self deign to look upon it. Rāma: [Gazes at it.]
"You know, dear boy, how to console the Queen when she is distressed. For how long must you do so?
Lakṣmaṇa:
"Until the noble lady’s purification by fire."
Rāma: Peace! (With words of consolation:
What need has she, who is purified by her very birth, of other purifiers?
The water of a sacred ford and fire do not deserve purity from any other source.

O Goddess, born from the sacrificial ground of the gods! Be gracious. This scandal shall last as long as you live. Indeed, those who are distressed must be conciliated by people; therefore, that which was spoken—both unpleasant and improper—is not fitting for you.

Śītā—(gazing intently) Who are these standing closely together above, as if offering praise to my noble lord? (Ka ete upari nirantarasthitā upastuvantīvāryaputram?)
Lakṣmaṇa:

My lady, these are those very Jṛmbhaka weapons along with their secret mantras, which were transmitted from the venerable Kṛśāśva to the sage Kauśika. He bestowed them upon Artha for the sake of slaying Tāṭakā.
Rāma:—
Worship, O Goddess, the divine weapons!
For the sake of the welfare of the Brahman, Brahmā and the other ancient preceptors performed austerities for more than a thousand autumns;
they beheld these very weapons, which are their own splendors composed of ascetic power.
Sītā:
Homage to them!
Rāma:—
"In every way, they shall now attend upon your offspring.
Sītā:
"I am favored."
Lakṣmaṇa:
This is the account of Mithilā. Sītā: [Listens]

Oh! How the noble son has been depicted—his gentle and beautiful splendor visible to his father’s eyes, which are fixed in wonder; his body possessing a fleshy beauty that is dark, glossy, smooth, and radiant like a blooming blue lotus; and his crest of peacock feathers adorning his charming face as he nonchalantly snaps Śiva’s bow.
Lakṣmaṇa:
Noble lady, look, look!
This father of yours honors his kinsmen, Vasiṣṭha and the others, as does Gautama Śatānanda, the family priest of the Janakas. (16)
Rāma:
This is most fitting. To whom is the alliance between the Janakas and the Raghus not dear?
Wherein the giver and the receiver were both the son of Kuśika himself. || 17 ||
Sītā: These four brothers of yours have indeed just performed the auspicious Godāna ceremony and are now consecrated for the marriage rites. Oh! I realize that I was present at that very time.
Rāma: [Listens]
O fair-faced one! That very time has returned, in which [the hand] offered by Gautama gladdened me;
this hand of yours, now grasping a beautiful bracelet, is like a great festival incarnate. (18)
Lakṣmaṇa:

This is my noble sister; this is also the noble Māṇḍavī; and this is the daughter-in-law Śrutakīrti. Sītā: (Note: The provided text fragment ends with "Sītā:", indicating that the following portion of the dialogue would have been spoken by her.)
Child, who else could this be?

Lakṣmaṇa: (With a bashful smile; aside) Ah, the Noble Lady is asking about Ūrmilā. Very well; I shall divert her attention elsewhere. (Aloud) Noble Lady, look! This is something worth seeing. And here is the venerable Mārgava.
Sītā— (With agitation) I am trembling!
Rāma—
"O Sage! Salutations to you!
Lakṣmaṇa:
"Noble Lady! Look! Here is the Noble One... (having spoken thus far).
Rāma—(With reproach) Ah! There is much more to be seen. Show me another way.
Sītā—
(Gazing with affection and great respect: You shine most brightly, noble son, by virtue of this greatness of your humility!
Lakṣmaṇa:
We have now arrived at Ayodhyā.
Rāma: I remember.
When my father was still living and my marriage was recent—
Indeed, those days of ours have passed while we were being cared for by our mothers.
At that time, this Jānakī too—bearing a child’s face with its charming, slightly opening locks of hair thin and sparse at the ends, and its flower-like teeth possessing a lovely luster;
she stirs my curiosity with her limbs, which possess a natural sweetness through their playful, shimmering movements and innocent, moon-like graces. (20)
Lakṣmaṇa:
This is the account of Mantharā.
Rāma: [Listens.]
(Quickly pointing elsewhere: Queen Vaidehī!
This is that very *iṅgudī* tree in the city of Śṛṅgavera-pura, where in former times there was a meeting with the affectionate lord of the Niṣādas.
Lakṣmaṇa:
(Smiling; to himself) Ah, the matter concerning my mother has been diverted by my noble brother. Sītā: [Continues]
Ah! This is the account of the binding of the matted locks.
Lakṣmaṇa:
That which was maintained by the aged Ikṣvākus, who had transferred their royal fortune to their sons—
In his youth, that noble one observed the meritorious vow of the forest-dweller.
Sītā: This is the divine Bhāgīrathī, whose waters are pure with merit. Rāma: O tutelary deity of the Raghu clan! Salutations to you.

O Blessed One! Having performed austerities that caused him no thought for his own body, Bhagīratha—after his father’s ancestors had been consumed by the wrathful splendor of Kapila during Sagara’s sacrifice while they were digging the earth in their search for the horse—finally delivered them by means of your waters once he had touched them. (23)
Therefore, O Mother, be as auspiciously attentive toward your daughter-in-law Sītā as Arundhatī is.
Lakṣmaṇa:
This is the banyan tree named Śyāma on the bank of the Kālindī, standing along the path leading to Citrakūṭa, which was pointed out by Bharadvāja. (Rāma gazes longingly.)
Sītā: Does my noble husband remember that place? Rāma: Oh, how could it be forgotten?
There, while on the journey, you were provided with massages by his relaxed, languid, and charming embraces—embraces that were slackened by the exhaustion of the road.
Where, having placed upon my chest your limbs, as frail as crushed lotus stalks, you attained sleep.
Lakṣmaṇa:
This is the account of the encounter with Virādha at the entrance of the Vindhya forest.
Sītā:—

Enough of this for now. Let me first observe my own grave danger—my status as a traveler on the path to the Southern Forest, while still holding the palm-leaf fan and parasol in the hands of my noble son.
Rāma:
These are those very penance groves on the banks of mountain torrents, where trees are inhabited by hermits.
In those [hermitages], self-restrained householders who cook only a handful of wild grain dwell in their homes, making hospitality their highest virtue.
Lakṣmaṇa:

This is the mountain named Prasravaṇa, situated in the midst of Janasthāna, its caves opening toward the Godāvarī which is embraced by a surrounding forest dense with thickets of trees; its dark-blue hue is intensified by clouds that are constantly pouring down rain.
Rāma:
Do you remember, O fair-limbed one, those days on that mountain when we were comforted by the hospitality provided by Lakṣmaṇa?
Do you remember the Godāvarī with its sweet waters, or do you remember our wanderings along its very banks? (26)

Moreover: As they whispered something, something very softly and indistinctly in turn, their cheeks pressed close together through the intensity of their passion, and with one arm each engaged in a firm embrace, the night itself came to an end before they were aware that the watches had passed. 27.
Lakṣmaṇa:
This is the dispute with Śūrpaṇakhā at Pañcavaṭī. Sītā: [Recognizing]—
"Alas, noble husband! This is all the sight I have of you!
Rāma:
O you who are terrified of separation! This is but a painting.
Sītā: Be that as it may, a wicked person causes unhappiness.
Rāma:—
Ah! The events of Janasthāna appear to me as if they were happening right now.
Lakṣmaṇa:
And this deed, performed by those wicked Rākṣasas through the ruse of the golden deer, pains me even though it has been washed away.
In the empty Janasthāna, even the stones weep and even the diamond splits, because of the noble deeds performed by those with impaired senses. (28)
Sītā—(With tears, to herself: Alas! Even he, the delight of the Solar dynasty, was thus exhausted on my account.
Lakṣmaṇa—
(Reflecting upon Rāma with significance) Noble brother! What is this?
Here, indeed, this stream of tears—like a string of pearls broken loose—rolls upon the earth in torrents, its drops shattered;
and though his agitation is suppressed, it becomes evident to others by the quivering of his lips and nostrils, as his heart has long been distended with grief. (29)
Rāma:
My child!

At that time, although the fire of grief born from separation from my beloved was intense, it was endured through the desire for retaliation; yet now, as it ripens once more within the mind, it spreads a pain like a wound in a vital organ. (30)
Sītā:
Alas, woe! Alas, woe! Even I, overcome by this excessive longing, perceive myself as if empty of my noble husband.
Lakṣmaṇa:

(To himself: Very well, I shall provoke him. (Gazing at the painting; aloud: Now, this is an illustration of the heroic exploits and deeds of the venerable father Jaṭāyu, whose life-span lasted through this entire Manvantara.
Sītā:
Alas, father! You have fulfilled your love for your offspring.
Rāma:
Alas, dear father, King of Birds, son of Kaśyapa! Where indeed could there be the birth of another such great, holy man, who has become a sacred ford for the world?
Lakṣmaṇa: [He speaks.]

This is that portion of the Daṇḍaka forest called Kuñjavana, situated to the west of Janasthāna and inhabited by the headless demon Danu. This is Mataṅga’s hermitage in its vicinity; there dwells a female ascetic of the Śabara tribe named Śramaṇā, who has attained perfection. And this is the lotus-lake known as Pampā, where it is said that my noble husband wept aloud, his fortitude shattered by indignation.
Sītā:
It was there, indeed, that my noble husband wept with a choked throat, his composure broken by grief.
Rāma:

O Queen, this lake is exceedingly beautiful. In it, amidst the intervals between the falling and rising of my tears, I beheld regions filled with blue lotuses, their broad stalks shimmering as they were shaken by the wings of mallikākṣa geese warbling with passion. (31)
Lakṣmaṇa:
Here is the noble Hanumān!
Sītā:—
This is that great-souled son of the Wind-god, who rendered a profound service by rescuing the world of the living from long ago.
Rāma:
By good fortune, here is that mighty-armed one, the increaser of Añjanā’s joy!
By whose valor we and the worlds have been made successful.
Sītā:

My child, what is the name of this mountain, where the peacocks dance among the blossoming *kadamba* trees, and where my noble husband—his beautiful splendor remaining only as a memory of his majesty and grace—was depicted by you while weeping, as he leaned against the foot of a tree in a faint?
Lakṣmaṇa: ...
This is that mountain named Mālyavat, fragrant with *kakubha* flowers, upon whose peak rests a fresh, dark, and glistening rain-cloud. Here, by my noble brother...
[Rāma: ...Stop, stop! I am no longer able to proceed; were I to turn back, it would be as if I were once again separated from Jānakī.

Beyond this, there are countless further and ever-greater miraculous deeds of our noble brother and those venerable Rākṣasas. Moreover, our noble lady is exhausted; therefore, I request that she rest.
Sītā: [Silent]
"Noble son! By means of this viewing of the paintings, there is something that must be made known to me, who am currently experiencing a pregnancy-longing.
Rāma: "Indeed, give your command."
Sītā: I know that once again, in the serene and deep forest groves, I shall bathe in the divine Bhāgīrathī, whose waters are eternally pure, stainless, and cool.
Rāma: [Listens]
"My child Lakṣmaṇa! Lakṣmaṇa: "Here I am!"

Sītā: [Listens.]
"Noble son! You too must come.
Rāma:
"O you of such cruel heart! Must even this be said?"
Sītā: In that case, it is pleasing to me.
Lakṣmaṇa:—
"As the noble one commands. (Exit.
Rāma:
My dear, lie down near the window.
Sītā: So be it. (She faints from the sleep of exhaustion.
Rāma:—
Therefore, hold me closely here for the sake of rest;

let this arm—resembling a necklace of moonstones dripping as they are kissed by the rays of the moon—be placed around my neck, as if to revive me with its drops of perspiration born of agitation and fatigue. (34)
(Acting thus with joy) My beloved! What is this?
Is it happiness or is it suffering? Is it delusion or sleep? Is it perhaps the spreading of poison, or is it intoxication?
For at every touch of yours, my entire collection of senses becomes utterly bewildered; this transformation both whirls my consciousness and causes it to close. (35)
Sītā:
It is indeed a marvel that you are so serene and composed!
Rāma: [Listens.]

O lotus-eyed one! These well-spoken words of yours cause the withered flower of life to bloom; they are nourishing, they enchant all the senses, they are nectar to the ears and an elixir for the mind. (36)
Sītā:
O sweet-spoken one! Come, let us lie down. (Thus she looks all around for a place to sleep.
Rāma:—
Ah! What more remains to be sought?

From the time of our marriage, whether at home or in the forest, first in childhood and thereafter in youth, this arm of Rāma—never resorted to by any other woman—is here to serve as your pillow for sleep. (37)
Sītā—(Acting as if falling asleep) This is it. Noble son! This is it. (She sleeps.
Rāma—
How is it that she, who speaks only such endearing words, is fast asleep upon my breast? (Gazing;
with affection) She is the Goddess of Fortune in my home; she is the wick of nectar for my eyes; this touch of hers upon my body is like abundant sandalwood paste;
this arm of hers around my neck is a cool and smooth string of pearls—what is there about her that is not dear to me? Only her separation is utterly unbearable. (38)
(Entering) The female doorkeeper:
Your Majesty! Rāma has arrived.
Ah! Who is it?
Portress:
It is Durmukha, the King’s personal attendant.

Rāma—(To himself) Durmukha is an attendant of the inner apartments. He has been dispatched by me as a spy among the citizens and country-folk. (Aloud) Let him enter. (The female door-keeper exits. (Entering) Durmukha—
(To himself) Alas! How shall I now report such inconceivable public scandal concerning the King in the absence of the Queen? Or rather, this is surely the duty of me, one of such meager fortune.
Sītā—(Talking in her sleep) Noble Lord! Where are you?
Rāma:
This very same longing, which causes such anxiety through the sight of the painting, is now inciting the Queen to an effort toward dreaming. (Tenderly touching her limbs:
That which persists in all conditions, transcending both pleasure and pain—[is this not she?]

Blessed is that fortunate man for whom there exists even a single instance of that which is sought after with such difficulty: a resting place for the heart where the essence of love remains unassailable by old age, matured through time until the veils have fallen away, and established in the very core of affection. (39)
Durmukha—
(Approaching) Victory to the King!
Rāma—
"Tell me what you have perceived. Durmukha replied: "The citizens and country-folk are praising Your Majesty, saying that we have been made to forget the great King Daśaratha by the divine Rāma."
Rāma: This is merely a figurative exaggeration. But tell me some fault of mine, so that it may be remedied.
Durmukha:
(With tears) (Into his ear) Let the Great King hear this! It is even so!
Rāma—Alas! This thunderbolt of speech is exceedingly sharp. (He faints.)
Durmukha:
May Your Majesty take heart.
Rāma: [Listens.]

(Sighing) Alas, alas! Woe is me! That stain of Vaidehī’s dwelling in another's house, which had been quelled by extraordinary means, has now, through the cruel turn of fate, spread once more on all sides like the venom of a rabid dog. (40)
So what shall I, unfortunate as I am, do today? (Reflecting, with compassion: Or rather, what is this?
For the propitiation of the world through some purpose is the highest duty for the virtuous;
indeed, that was understood by my father when he abandoned me and his own life. (41)
And just now, the venerable Vasiṣṭha has sent this message:

"Moreover, this noble and wonderful conduct, which has been illuminated by the best of men, the protectors of the earth, who are sons of the Sun—if, through my connection with it, a foul rumor should arise, alas! Fie upon me, the unfortunate one! (42)

Alas, O Queen, born from the sacrificial ground! Alas, O you who have sanctified the earth by the grace of your own birth! Alas, daughter of Janaka! Alas, you whose character was praised by Agni, Vasiṣṭha, and Arundhatī! Alas, whose life was filled with Rāma! Alas, dear companion of the forest-dwelling! Alas, beloved of our father! Alas, you of so few words! How can such a transformation have come upon you, who are so noble?
By you the worlds were made holy; yet upon you fall the unholy words of men.
By you the people have their protector; now, left without a protector, you shall perish. (43)
(To Durmukha) Durmukha! Tell Lakṣmaṇa: "This new king Rāma issues this command. (Into his ear) "Just so, just so. Durmukha:
Alas! How is it that the King has resolved upon this based on the words of a wicked man, regarding the Queen who was purified by fire and whose lineage is sanctified by the child within her womb?
Rāma:
Heaven forbid! Heaven forbid! Are the citizens and country-folk truly called "wicked"?
The lineage of Ikṣvāku is beloved by the subjects, and by fate, its seed has become subject to reproach.
And as for that wondrous deed at the time of purification—who could believe it, if it had occurred long ago? (44)
Therefore, depart.
Durmukha: "Alas! O Queen! (Thus he exits.)
Rāma:
Alas, what misery! I have become a cruel man of most loathsome deeds.
Having nurtured from childhood this beloved one, who shared my very dwelling, how can I— [abandon her]?
Under a pretext, I deliver myself to death, like a little bird in the house to a butcher. ||45||
So why should I, though untouchable and a sinner, defile the Goddess? (Thus raising Sītā’s head and pulling her arm:
O innocent one! Release me, you wretched outcaste of unprecedented deeds!
You have clung to a poisonous tree of bitter fruit, mistaking it for sandalwood. 46.

(Rising) Alas, alas! The world of living beings has now been overturned. Today the purpose of Rāma’s life has come to an end. Now the world is a desolate, withered forest; existence is without essence; the body is but wood; I am without refuge. What shall I do? What is my course? Or rather:
consciousness has returned to Rāma only for the experience of suffering;
his life-breaths, striking at his vital organs, have become like bolts of adamant.

Alas, Mother Arundhatī! Venerable Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra! Blessed Fire-god! Alas, Goddess Earth, the Sustainer of Beings! Alas, Father Janaka! Alas, Mother! Alas, dear friend, the Great King Sugrīva! Gentle Hanumān! Benefactor, Lord of Laṅkā, Vibhīṣaṇa! Alas, friend Trijaṭā! You have been robbed; you have been insulted by this wretched Rāma. Or rather, who indeed am I now to call upon them?
For I believe those great souls, when their names are seized by me—a thankless and evil-souled man—are as if touched by sin itself. (48)
I, who out of confidence have cast off my dear wife— the very goddess of the household— who has fallen asleep upon my chest,
am as cruel as a beast of prey as I hurl her, heavy with a fetus throbbing in its distress, like a sacrificial offering to the flesh-eaters. (49)
(Placing Sītā’s feet upon his head: This is the last time that your lotus-feet shall touch the head of Rāma. (He weeps. (Offstage:
A sacrilege! A sacrilege!
Rāma:

"O sir! Let it be known: what is this? (Again, from behind the scenes: "The multitude of sages dwelling on the banks of the Yamunā, performing fierce austerities, terrified by Lavaṇa, has approached you for protection. (50)
Rāma:

How can there still be fear of Rākṣasas today? Therefore, I shall dispatch Śatrughna to uproot this wicked-souled son of Kumbhīnasī from Mādhura. (Walking about, then turning back) Alas, Queen! How will you depart in such a state? Blessed Vasundharā! Behold your most praiseworthy daughter, Jānakī—she who is the entire auspiciousness of the lineages of the Janakas and the Raghus.
Her whom you begot at a holy place of sacrifice, she who is herself of virtuous character. ||51||
(Thus he exits weeping.

Sītā: Alas, gentle noble son! Where are you? Alas, woe! Woe! Deceived by the ominous throbbing of a bad dream, I see myself as if empty of my noble son. Alas, woe! Woe! Having abandoned me while I slept alone, where has my lord gone? Very well; I shall be angry with him, if only I can master myself while looking for him. Who is there? (Entering:)
Durmukha:
My Queen! Prince Lakṣmaṇa reports that the chariot is ready; therefore, may Your Majesty ascend it. Sītā:—
(Rising and walking about) Here I have ascended. My womb throbs with its burden. Let us proceed slowly. Durmukha:
This way, this way, Your Majesty!
Sītā:
Homage to the deities of the Raghu dynasty! (Thus they all exit.
Thus ends the first act, titled "The Vision of the Painting," in the *Uttararāmacarita* composed by the great poet Śrī Bhavabhūti.
Forest Deity—(Scattering the water of honor):
This forest is for you to enjoy as you please; this is a blessed day for me, for association with the virtuous occurs only through some measure of merit.
The shade of trees, water, and even the food appropriate for ascetics—whether fruit or root—that too is not dependent on others here for you.
Ascetic:
What more can be said here?
Her conduct is for the most part pleasing; her restraint in speech is sweet with modesty; her mind is naturally auspicious; and her acquaintance is beyond reproach.
Whether before or after, this secret of the virtuous—whose essence is unaltered, free from artifice, and pure—triumphs. ||2||
(As they sit down) The Forest Deity: But who might this lady be that I perceive here?
Ascetic: I am Ātreyī.
Forest Deity:
"Noble Ātreyī! From where have you come here? What is the purpose of your wandering through the groves of the Daṇḍaka forest?
Ātreyī:
"In this region, many masters of the *udgītha* reside, headed by Agastya."
To acquire from them the knowledge of the Upanishads, I am wandering here from the presence of Vālmīki. ||3||
Forest Deity:
Since even other sages formerly attended upon that very seer Prācetasa, the ancient expounder of the Veda, for the purpose of studying the Brahman, what is this journey of the noble lady?
Ātreyī:
For this long absence has been accepted because of that great obstacle to study.
Forest Deity:
Of what sort is it?
Ātreyī:

There, a certain distinguished deity presented to the Blessed One two children—who were in a state of wonder at every turn—at an age when they had only just been weaned. Indeed, that [event] does not merely affect his own heart, but it also causes the inner hearts of even animals to overflow with affection for the truth.
Forest Deity:
"Do they even have names? Ātreyī:
"Indeed, it was said by the deity that their names are Kuśa and Lava, as well as their power."
Forest Deity:
Of what nature is his power?
Ātreyī:
"It is said that the *jṛmbhakāstra*s, along with their secret mantras, were born with them.
Vanadevatā:
"Oh, how truly marvelous this is!"
Ātreyī:

Those two were taken by the venerable Vālmīki from the service of a nurse and nourished and protected by him. Once their *caula* ceremony was performed, he diligently brought them to mastery in the three other branches of knowledge, excluding the triple Veda (*trayī*). Thereafter, when they reached their eleventh year, the venerable one initiated them according to the Kṣatriya rite and instructed them in the triple Veda. However, because of their exceedingly radiant intelligence, there is no possibility of joint study for those such as ourselves with these two. For:
A teacher imparts knowledge to both the wise and the dull-witted alike; yet he neither bestows nor withholds the capacity for understanding in them.
Nevertheless, there is indeed a vast difference regarding the result: just as a pure gem is capable of reflecting an image, whereas clay and the like are not. (4)
Forest Deity: Is this an obstacle to your studies? Ātreyī: [Yes.]
And another:
the forest deity—
then who is this other one?
Ātreyī:

Now, on one occasion, that Brahmarṣi, having approached the river Tamasā for the midday libation, saw there one of a pair of *krauñca* birds being struck by a hunter. He uttered a divine voice, appearing spontaneously, transformed into the *anuṣṭubh* meter:
"O Niṣāda! May you find no firm footing for eternal years!"
In that you killed one of a pair of cranes while it was deluded by passion. (5)
Forest Deity:
A painting? A novel introduction of meters other than those handed down by tradition!
Ātreyī: [She speaks.]

Then, at that time, the Blessed One who originates all beings, the lotus-born Brahmā, approached that Ṛṣi whose voice had manifested as a revelation and said: "O Ṛṣi! You have awakened to the Brahman which is the self of speech. Therefore, speak the life-story of Rāma. May your prophetic vision, with its unimpeded light, be revealed to you; you are the primal poet. Having spoken thus, he vanished.
Then that blessed son of Pracetas composed the *Rāmāyaṇa*, an epic history which is such a manifestation of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) among men for the first time.
The Forest Deity:
Alas! Saṃsāra is a wise man. Ātreyī:
That is precisely why I say, "In that regard, there is a great obstacle to study."
Forest Deity:
It is fitting.
Ātreyī:
"I am rested, my dear lady! Now, please tell me the way to Agastya’s hermitage.
Forest Deity:
"Having entered Pañcavaṭī from here, you may proceed along this bank of the Godāvarī."
Ātreyī—(tearfully) Is this the grove of asceticism? Is this Pañcavaṭī? Is this the river Godāvarī? Is this Mount Prasravaṇa? And are you Vāsantī, the forest deity of Janasthāna?
Forest Deity—
It is exactly so; all of that is true. Ātreyī:
Alas, my child Jānakī!
This very circle of your beloved kinsmen is the subject of these incidental stories;
even though you exist only as a name, their being seen makes you appear to us as if you were perceived before our very eyes.
Vāsantī—(With fear; to herself) How is it that he speaks as if she were nothing but a name? (Aloud) Is some great calamity befallen Queen Sītā?
Ātreyī—
Not only is it a great calamity, but it is also accompanied by reproach. (Into her ear: "So be it.
Vāsantī: Alas! What a cruel stroke of fate! (She faints.)
Ātreyī: My good lady, take heart, take heart! Vāsantī:

Alas, dear friend! Such is the portion of your creation. Alas, dear Rāmabhadra! Or rather, enough of you. Ātreyī! Now, after Lakṣmaṇa had departed from that forest, leaving her behind, is there any news as to what happened to Sītā?
Ātreyī: No, indeed not.
Vāsantī: Alas! While our families are presided over by the noble Arundhatī and Vasiṣṭha, and while the aged queens are still living, how has this come to pass?
Ātreyī: [She speaks.]

At that time, the elders were present at the sacrifice of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga; now the sacrifice has been completed. Having honored them, the elders have been dismissed by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga. Then the venerable Arundhatī said, "I will not go to Ayodhyā separated from my daughter-in-law. That very sentiment was approved by Rāma’s mothers. Out of deference to her, the venerable Vasiṣṭha also resolved, "We shall go and dwell in the forest of Vālmīki.
Vāsantī: And what is the conduct of that noble Rāma?
Ātreyī:
That king has commenced the royal horse-sacrifice, the Aśvamedha.
Vāsantī:
Ahaha, alas! Married even?
Ātreyī: Peace! No, no.
Vāsantī:
Who then is the partner in dharma at the sacrifice?
Ātreyī: [She is] the daughter of Atri.
A golden image of Sītā has been made into a housewife. Vāsantī:
Alas, oh!
Harder even than a diamond and softer even than a flower—who indeed is capable of understanding the minds of those who have transcended the world? ||7||
Ātreyī:

And the sacrificial horse has been released, consecrated by Vāmadeva; and its guardians have been appointed according to the scriptures. Their leader, Candraketu—the son of Lakṣmaṇa—has been dispatched accompanied by a fourfold army and entrusted with the transmission of divine weapons.
Vāsantī:
(With tears of joy and wonder) O Mother! Even Prince Lakṣmaṇa has a son! I am alive!
Ātreyī:

In the meantime, a Brahmin, having lifted up his deceased son at the palace gate, cried out "An outrage against the Brahmins! with beating of his breast. Then, while the compassionate Rāmabhadra was reflecting upon his own faults—thinking that untimely death does not befall subjects except through some transgression by the king—a bodiless voice suddenly rang out.
O Rāma, a low-caste man named Śambūka is performing austerities on this earth;
he is to be beheaded by you—slay him and restore the brahmin to life. (8)
Having heard this, the Lord of the World, sword in hand, ascended the Puṣpaka chariot and began a search in all directions and intermediate points to find the Śūdra ascetic.
Vāsantī:
A Śūdra named Śambūka, who inhales smoke with his face turned downwards, is practicing austerities right here in Janasthāna. Might the noble Rāma perhaps adorn this forest once again?
Ātreyī: Noble lady, let us go now. Vāsantī:

Noble Ātreyī! So be it. The day is indeed harsh. For instance: The trees on the banks of the Godāvarī worship the river with flowers whose stalks have loosened due to the heat, falling as they are shaken by the rubbing of the temples of elephants itching for a scratch; meanwhile, the nesting trees on the bank resound with flocks of weary pigeons and wild cocks, while the insects emerging from their bark are pecked at by the beaks of birds scratching in the shade. (9)
(Thus, having walked about, they exit. This concludes the pure *viṣkambhaka*. (Then enters Rāmabhadra with his sword raised mercifully.
Rāma:
O right hand! Release the sword upon the Śūdra ascetic for the sake of restoring life to the deceased Brahmin child.
You are the arm of Rāma, skilled in banishing Sītā when she was exhausted by her heavy pregnancy; how can there be compassion in you? ||10||
(Somehow) a deed worthy of Rāma has been performed. Might that son of a Brāhmaṇa still live? (Entering) A Divine Being:
Victory to Your Majesty!
While you, the wielder of the rod of punishment, have granted immunity even from Yama, this child has been restored to life, as has this prosperity of mine.
O Śambūka, here I am, bowing my head at your feet;
even deaths born of association with the virtuous lead one across [the ocean of existence]. 11.
Rāma:
Both are pleasing to us; therefore, experience the fruition of your severe asceticism—that wherein there are joys and delights, and wherein there are holy riches.
May those worlds named Vairāja, which are radiant, be auspicious for you. ||12||
Śambūka:

My lord! This greatness is due solely to your grace; what need is there for asceticism here? Or rather, great indeed has been the service rendered by my penance, since you, the Lord of the World and the refuge of all, whom one must seek throughout the universe, have come seeking me, a mere low-born man (vṛṣalaka), across hundreds of yojanas.
Having traversed [the distance], he has arrived here through the power of his asceticism; otherwise, how could there be for you this return from Daṇḍaka forest to Ayodhyā? (13)
Rāma:

What, is this Daṇḍaka forest? (Looking all around) Alas! How is it that these familiar regions of the Daṇḍaka wilderness are now visible—some parts dark and glossy, others elsewhere harsh with terrifying expanses, their quarters made resonant here and there by the gurgling of waterfalls, interspersed with sacred fords, hermitages, mountains, rivers, ravines, and forests? ||14||
Śambūka:
This is indeed Daṇḍakāraṇya. It is said that formerly, while the Lord was dwelling here, fourteen thousand and fourteen Rākṣasas [were slain].
And were not the three—Dūṣaṇa, Khara, and Triśiras—slain by you in battle? ||15||
By which [act] the movement of even common folk like me has become free from fear in this sacred field of accomplishment (*siddhakṣetra*).
Rāma:
Is it not only Daṇḍakā, but Janasthāna as well?
Śambūka:

Indeed! These long forests bordering Janasthāna, which cause the hair of all living beings to stand on end, and whose formidable mountain caves are overrun by packs of mad and fierce beasts, are indeed turning toward the southern direction. For instance:
in some places they are silent and still, while in others there are the cries of fierce creatures; in them, fires are kindled by the breath of deep-bodied serpents sleeping at their own will.
In the hollows of the ravines along the boundaries, where there is but scant and sparse water, even the *pratisūryaka* insects, parched with thirst, drink the sweat-fluid of the pythons.
Rāma:
I behold Janasthāna, the former abode of Khara;
I experience the past events as if they were present before my eyes. (17)
(Looking all around) Vaidehī was fond of gardens; these, indeed, are but wildernesses. What could be more terrifying than this?
(With tears) "I shall dwell with you in the forests fragrant with honey"—even as she spoke thus, her affection for him was of such a nature that she found delight therein. (18)
Without performing even the slightest action, one dispels sufferings through joys;
for that person who is dear to someone is indeed that person's very substance.
Śambūka:

Therefore, enough with these inaccessible [regions]. Now, let the noble sir behold these great forests—tranquil and profound, providing refuge for herds of wild beasts, adorned with clusters of trees whose dense, dark shadows are cast by borders strewn with the soft plumage of peacocks warbling with passion;
here flow rivers of cool, clear water, fragrant with the blossoms shed from cane thickets frequented by intoxicated birds.
There are mountain streams whose many currents are made resonant by stumbling through groves of rose-apple trees dark with the ripening of their heavy fruit.
Moreover:
Here, the deep, resonant bellows of young bears dwelling in the caves grow heavy and thick;
and the cold, pungent, and astringent scent of the exudations from the joints of *sallakī* trees, torn open and scattered by elephants, spreads abroad. (21)
Rāma—(With a choked voice) Good man! May your paths leading to the gods be auspicious. You are departing from the worlds of merit.
Śambūka—
"Until, having saluted the ancient Brahman-sage Agastya, I enter the eternal state. (Thus he exits.
Rāma:
Oh, how is it that I see this forest again today, in which we dwelt for so long in the past?

Both forest-dwellers and householders are devoted to their own duties; as for us, we are connoisseurs of the pleasures of worldly existence. These are those very same mountains with their warbling peacocks, those same forest regions with their intoxicated deer, and those same riverbanks with their lovely *vañjula* creepers and dense thickets of *nicula* reeds.
This mountain which appears as if from afar like a mass of clouds is Prasravaṇa; here flows the river Godāvarī.
On a great peak of this very mountain was the dwelling of the king of vultures; beneath it, we too took delight in those leaf-huts.
There, the lovely forest edge—dark with the beauty of spreading trees, resonant with the warbling of birds within—lay along the waters of the Godāvarī. (25)

Right here is that Pañcavaṭī, where the various regions bear witness to our many intimate confidences through our dwelling; and there is Vāsantī, the forest deity and dear friend of my beloved. What has befallen Rāma today? For now, as it were, a sharp poison spreads after a long time, beginning its onset with violent force; like a fragment of a splinter shaken loose from some internal agitation;
like a scarred-over wound bursting open again upon a vital organ—this old grief, having become as if new, overwhelms me with its agitation. (26)

I still see such regions of the earth as they were in former times. (Observing closely) The arrangement of living beings is unstable. For instance: where formerly there was a stream, now there is a sandbank; where there was a sandbank, now there is a stream. The density and sparseness of the trees have undergone a reversal. Having seen it for a long time, I consider this forest to be like another altogether; yet, the presence of these mountains makes me firm in the conviction that "this is indeed that very place."

Alas, alas! Even as I seek to avoid it, Pañcavaṭī seems to draw me toward her by force through its own affection. (With pathos) How can that sinful Rāma—now alone, having lost his beloved—either look upon or pass by that very Pañcavaṭī, where those days were spent with her as if in our own home, and which was constantly made to seem long only by the stories concerning her? || 28 ||
(Entering) Śambūka:

Victory to the King! The venerable Agastya, having heard of your presence from me, says to you: "The affectionate Lopāmudrā, having performed the auspicious rites of consecration, awaits you, as do all the great sages. Therefore, come; honor us. Then, having reached your own country by means of the swift Puṣpaka, prepare for the horse sacrifice.
Rāma: [Listens.]
"As the Blessed One commands.
Śambūka:
This way, this way, Your Majesty!
Rāma—(Setting the Puṣpaka in motion) O venerable Pañcavaṭī! For the sake of complying with the command of my elders, may this transgression of Rāma be forgiven for a moment.
Śambūka—

O King! Behold this mountain named Krauñca, where the flocks of birds are silenced by the tumultuous whistling of the hollow bamboo stalks, which resembles the hissing of swarms of owls in the humming bowers of the groves.
Here, upon the trunks of ancient *rohiṇa* trees, serpents writhe, agitated by the warbling of the peacocks as they move about.
Moreover,
these are those southern mountains whose dark peaks have their summits embraced by clouds, and whose valleys resound with the faltering murmur of the Godāvarī’s currents;
and these are those holy confluences of rivers with deep waters, tumultuous with the clamor of waves tossing against one another like stakes.
(Thus they all exit.
Thus ends the second act, titled "The Entrance into Pañcavaṭī," in the *Uttararāmacarita* composed by the great poet Śrī Bhavabhūti. || 2 ||
(Then enter two rivers.
One:
Friend Muralā! Why do you appear so agitated?
Muralā:

Friend Tamasā! I have been sent by Lopāmudrā, the wife of the venerable Agastya, to address the Godāvarī, the best of rivers. You surely know how, since the abandonment of her daughter-in-law, she has remained unexpressed due to her depth, with a dense anguish hidden within.
The pathetic sentiment (karuṇa-rasa) of Rāma is like a medicinal preparation cooked in a sealed vessel (puṭapāka). || 1 ||

And by this long succession of grief, arising from the calamitous downfall of such beloved kinsmen and producing an exceedingly choked voice, Rāmabhadra is now utterly exhausted. Beholding him, my heart trembles like a flower with its stalks weakly bound. And now, as Rāmabhadra returns, he will certainly behold those regions in the Pañcavaṭī forest that witnessed the confidence shared during his dwelling with his bride.

And in such a state, even for one naturally steadfast, there are at every step grounds for great negligence and objects of grief that must be feared, due to the agitation and intensity of a sorrow so profound in its reach. Therefore, O Blessed Godāvarī! You, being venerable, must remain vigilant.

"O Goddess, with breezes from your waves, cool with sprays of water-droplets, drawing along the fragrance of lotus filaments—by these winds sent forth ever so gently, satisfy the life-breath of the noble Rāma whenever he faints. (2)
Tamasā:
Kindness is indeed appropriate for affection. However, the means of restoring [him] to life is already present at the very root of Rāmabhadra’s being.
Muralā:
How so?

Listen to all of this: Long ago, it is said, when Lakṣmaṇa had departed after leaving her near the hermitage of Vālmīki, Queen Sītā, overcome by the intense agony of childbirth and the shock of extreme suffering, cast herself into the current of the Gaṅgā. At that very moment, she gave birth there to a pair of boys; she was then sustained by both the divine goddesses Pṛthvī and Bhāgīrathī and led down to the subterranean realm (Rasātala).
After the weaning from the breast, the two children were personally entrusted by the goddess Gaṅgā to that great seer Pracetasa.
Muralā—(with astonishment):
Even for such as these, the fruition [of karma] occurs as something most wonderful.
Where such a person as this becomes merely an instrument. || 3 ||
Tamasā:

Now, having heard from the mouth of the Sarayū that Rāmabhadra has reached Janasthāna following this incident of Śambūka, the venerable Bhāgīrathī, suspecting exactly what Lopāmudrā had suspected out of affection, has come to the Godāvarī accompanied by Sītā under some pretext of domestic duties.
Muralā: [Listens.]

The Blessed Bhāgīrathī has thought most profoundly: "For this dear Rāma, who stands established in statecraft and is occupied with various affairs for the prosperity of the worlds, distractions of mind are inevitable. But for him, when undistracted and accompanied only by his grief, entry into Pañcavaṭī would be a great calamity. How, then, might Sītā console this dear Rāma?
Tamasā—

The blessed Bhāgīrathī has already said: "Child Sītā, born from the sacrificial ground! Today indeed the auspicious knot marking the twelfth year of the lives of the long-lived Kuśa and Lava is reached. Therefore, worship with flowers gathered by your own hands the god Savitṛ, the ancient father-in-law of yours and the progenitor of this entire lineage of royal seers of Manu’s race, so that you may be cleansed of all sin."

"Even the forest deities shall not see you as you stand upon the surface of the earth by our power, much less mortals. I too was thus commanded: "Tamasa! Janaki is truly devoted to you; therefore, you yourself must become her constant companion. As such, I am now carrying out what has been instructed.
Murala:
I too shall report this news to the venerable Lopamudra. I suspect that Ramabhadra has already arrived.
Tamasā:
This very Godāvarī, having emerged from her pool,
bears a face beautiful with cheeks that are exceedingly pale and emaciated, and with its disheveled tresses tossing about.
Or is Janaki the very embodiment of compassion, or perhaps the personified agony of separation, who has come to the forest? || 4 ||
Muralā:

This is indeed she, whose lovely body—like a tender sprout severed from its bond—is being withered by a cruel and long-lasting grief that parches her heart-lotus; it has become pale and emaciated, like the inner petal of a *ketakī* flower scorched by the autumn heat. (Having walked about, they both exit.)
Thus ends the pure *viṣkambhaka*. (Behind the scenes: "Child! Child! (Then enters Sītā, busy gathering flowers, listening with both compassion and eagerness.
Sītā:
Ah, I know it is my dear friend Vāsantī who speaks. (Again, behind the scenes:
That young elephant calf, which was formerly reared by Queen Sītā with the tips of sallakī shoots held in her own hands, is now restless before [the lion].
Sītā:
What of him? (Again, behind the scenes:
While sporting with his mate, he has been encountered and attacked by another, a lordly elephant of unrestrained pride. || 6 ||

Sītā—(With agitation, having walked a few steps) Noble husband! Save him, save my little son! Alas, alas! Those very same syllables, long familiar to me, now bind me, unfortunate as I am, with the sight of Pañcavaṭī. Oh, noble husband! (Entering) Tamasā—
"Take heart, take heart! (Behind the scenes) "O King of Vimānas! Please remain right here.

Sītā—(With agitation and joy) Oh, from where does this deep and resonant sound of speech come, as grave as the thundering of clouds heavy with rain? It suddenly fills my ears and makes even me, unfortunate as I am, feel a sudden longing.
Tamasā—(With a smile and tears) Oh, child! Even at a sound whose origin is unclear and indistinct, you stand thus, startled and longing, like a peahen at the roar of thunder.
Sītā:
Noble lady, what are you saying? It is not clear. By the combination of the sounds, I recognize it; surely this was uttered by my noble husband himself.
Tamasā: [She speaks.]
"It is heard that the King of the Ikṣvāku line has come to the Daṇḍaka forest for the purpose of inflicting punishment upon a Śūdra who was performing austerities. Sītā:
"By good fortune, that king has not failed in his duty. (From behind the scenes:)
Where even the trees and the deer were my kinsmen, and where I dwelt for a long time with my beloved companion—
these are those very slopes of the mountain bordering the Godāvarī, abounding in many caves and waterfalls.

Sītā—(Embracing Tamasā, faints) By good fortune, my noble husband is recognizable only by his own gentle and profound majesty through his form, which is pale, emaciated, and weak like the orb of the moon at dawn. Blessed Tamasā! Support me!
Tamasā—

Child! Take heart, take heart! (Behind the scenes: By this sight of Pañcavaṭī, a fainting fit first envelops me like a surge of smoke from the fire of grief lying within, which is now about to blaze forth violently.
"Alas, dear Jānakī!
Tamasā—
(to herself) This is indeed what was foreseen by my elders.
Sītā—(Recovering her breath) Alas! How can this be? (Again, behind the scenes) Alas, Queen, dear companion of my residence in the Daṇḍaka forest, Princess of Videha! (She faints.
Sītā—

(Thus she falls at her feet) Alas, woe! Alas, woe! My ill-fated self—he with eyes like closed blue lotuses, has indeed fainted! Oh! How is he fallen upon the surface of the earth, overcome by the exhaustion of his suppressed breath? O Blessed Tamasā! Save him, save him! Give life to my noble son!
Tamasā:
Surely you yourself, O auspicious lady, must restore the Lord of the World to life!
For your hand has a pleasant touch; people are devoted to it for that reason. || 10 ||
Sītā:

Let it be as it may; I shall do as the venerable lady commands. (She exits in haste. (Then enters Rāma, fallen upon the ground, being touched by Sītā who is shedding tears, and breathing with joy. Sītā:
(With some joy) I feel as if the life of the three worlds has returned once more.
Rāma:
Alas, sir! What is this?
Is it perhaps a sprinkling of the juice from the sprouts of yellow sandalwood, or a drenching born from the squeezed stalks of moonbeams?
Ah! Is this elixir of the life-restoring herb, which refreshes the mind and sustains weary life, now present? (11)
Moreover, this touch is surely the same one familiar from before; it is the very thing that revives the mind and brings it satisfaction.
For it instantly dispels the fainting born of anguish and once again spreads a numbness through its bliss.
Sītā—
(Approaching with agitation and compassion) This alone is now more than enough for me.
Rāma—
(Sitting down) Have I not indeed been favored by the Queen, who is so affectionate toward her child?
Sītā:
Alas, woe! Woe! Why will my noble husband seek me out?
Rāma:
Very well, I shall see.
Sītā: [speaks]
O Blessed Tamasā! Let us depart for now; having seen me, the King will become even more incensed by my presence without permission.
Tamasā: Oh child! By the grace of Bhāgīrathī, you have become invisible even to the forest deities.
Sītā:
Is this indeed so?
Rāma: [It is.]

"Alas, my beloved Jānakī! Sītā—(With a voice choked with grief) Noble son! This is truly unworthy of such a turn of events. Blessed one, why shall I be so pitiless toward my noble son, who is so affectionate and speaks thus, even though he is one whose sight was once thought impossible and difficult to obtain again, even in other births? Why, directed specifically at me, the most unfortunate of women, shall I be heartless? I alone know his compassion; he is mine.
Rāma—(Looking all around with despondency: Alas! There is nothing here at all.
Sītā—
"O Blessed One! I do not know, I do not know what state of compassion I am in merely by the sight of this man who has renounced everything without cause!
Tamasā said: "I know, my child! I know!"

Your heart, which was indifferent due to despair, turbid from the influence of unpleasantness, and as if paralyzed by the sudden occurrence of this long separation, has in a single moment become clear through your goodness, deeply pained by the piteous cries of your beloved, and melted with love. (13)
Rāma:
O Queen!
Your touch is like grace incarnate—cool and moist with affection.
Even now you continue to gladden me; but where are you, O daughter? || 14 ||
Sītā:

Indeed, these are the playful utterances of my noble husband—utterances that display a wealth of affection from his unfathomable heart, which overflow with joy and consist of nectar. I know that, because of this conviction, even though my life was pierced by the thorn of being abandoned without cause, my very birth is held in high esteem by me.
Rāma: [Listens.]

Or rather, whence could there be a beloved? This must surely be a delusion of the noble Rāma, produced by the intensity of his habitual mental construction. (Behind the scenes: Oh! What a great oversight! An oversight! (The second half-verse beginning with "By Sītā-devī’s own hands... is recited.
Rāma—(With piteous longing: What of him? (Again behind the scenes, the latter half-verse beginning with "Together with his wife" is recited.)
Sītā:
Who is being addressed now?
Rāma: [He speaks.]
Who is this evil-souled man, who overcomes the son of my beloved, accompanied by his daughter-in-law? (He rises.
(Entering) Vāsantī—(Agitated) My Lord! Haste must be made!
Sītā: Alas! How is it my dear friend Vāsantī?
Rāma: [He looks.]
"How is Vāsantī, the dear friend of the Queen? Vāsantī:
"My Lord, hurry, hurry! To the south of this Jaṭāyu Peak, by way of the Sītā ford, let Your Majesty approach the Godāvarī and pay homage to the Queen’s little son."
Sītā:
Alas, dear Jaṭāyu! This Janasthāna is desolate without you.
Rāma: [Listens.]
Ahaha! These introductions to the story are truly cutting to the quick of my compassion.
Vāsantī:
This way, this way, Your Majesty.
Sītā: Blessed lady! It is indeed true that even the forest deity does not see me.
Tamasā:
O child! The sovereignty of Mandākinī is far superior to that of all other deities. Why, then, do you hesitate?
Sītā: Then let us follow her. (She walks about.)
Rāma—(Walking about) O blessed Godāvarī! Salutations to you!
Vāsantī—
(Reflecting) O King, rejoice with the victorious little son of the Queen, accompanied by his bride!
Rāma:
May the long-lived one be victorious!
Sītā:
Oh! My little son has become such a man!
Rāma: [Continues]
O Queen! Congratulations, you are prospering by good fortune!

O fair-limbed one, that very son of yours—who, with the tender sprout-like teeth emerging like fresh lotus shoots, pulled away the lavalī bud from the base of your ear—has now become the vessel for such auspiciousness as to be the conqueror of elephants in rut during his youth. (15)
Sītā:
May he now remain inseparable from this one of gentle appearance and long life.
Rāma: [Listens.]

Friend Vāsantī! Look, look! Even the skill in following his beloved has been learned by my dear child. He has mastered the practice of taking mouthfuls of lotus-stalks playfully uprooted, and he has perfected the transfer of mouthfuls of water scented with blooming lotuses.
At the end of these, he has freely provided a sprinkling with his trunk that sprays fine droplets; furthermore, out of affection, he holds over him a parasol made of uncurved lotus leaves.

Sītā: Venerable Tamasā! This man has indeed become such as you see. But as for those two, Kuśa and Lava, I do not know what they have become after all this time. Tamasā: [To herself] Alas, how great is the power of destiny! How can it be that she does not recognize her own sons? [Aloud] Noble lady, do not grieve. They have grown up in the hermitage of the sage Vālmīki, having been brought there by me. And now, having heard the *Rāmāyaṇa* from his own mouth, they have come here to behold their father. It is for this reason that the venerable Vālmīki has sent me to you. Therefore, noble lady, compose yourself. I shall lead them both here. [She exits. Sītā: [With tears] O blessed one, please bring them quickly. I cannot endure this separation from my children for even a moment longer. [She faints. Rāma: [Approaching] Noble lady, take heart, take heart! [He sprinkles water on her face. Sītā: [Regaining consciousness] My lord, where are my two children? Rāma: [Looking ahead] Noble lady, look at these two boys playing with the young deer in the hermitage. Sītā: [Looking with longing] My lord, they are indeed like my own sons. [She faints again. Rāma: [Sprinkling water on her face] Noble lady, take heart, take heart! Sītā: [Regaining consciousness] My lord, please show me my two children. As he is, so too are those two.
Sītā:
I am such an unfortunate woman that not only is there separation from my noble husband, but there is also separation from my sons.
Tamasā:
Such must this destiny be.
Sītā: [Listens.]

Or what is the use of me having given birth, since my noble husband has not kissed this pair of lotus-faces of my two little sons—faces so radiant with the slightly sparse, white buds of their teeth, graced by continuous, charming, sweet laughter, and ever-bright?
Tamasā: May it be so through the grace of the deity.
Sītā:

O venerable Tamasā! With my breasts swelling and overflowing with milk at this recollection of my children, I have for a moment become a partaker of worldly existence through the presence of my two dear ones’ father.
Tamasā:

What is said in this regard? Procreation is indeed the ultimate limit of affection. Moreover, this mutual union of the parents arises from the affection residing in the inner essence (*antahkarana-tattva*) of the couple. It is taught that "offspring" is this single knot of bliss. (17)
Vāsantī:
Your Majesty, look even further than this:
your beloved nurtured that [creeper] whose young, trembling shoots had only recently emerged, day after day.
Like a cresting jewel upon a crown, this peacock, accompanied by his mate, calls out from the kadamba tree.
Sītā— (With curiosity, affection, and tears) This is he!
Rāma—
"Rejoice, my child! We are celebrating today.
Sītā: "So be it."
Rāma:

I remember you with an affectionate heart, as if you were my own son, being made to dance by that charming girl who adorns herself with the rhythmic tapping of her bud-like hands and the wild dances of her flickering brows, while her eyes move in circular orbits within their sockets during her whirling turns.
Ah! Even animals respond to familiarity. This kadamba tree, which has put forth only a few blossoms, was once nurtured by my beloved.
Sītā—(tearfully)—My noble husband has recognized it perfectly.
Rāma:
This mountain peacock remembers the Queen, for he experiences joy here as if toward a kinsman. || 20 ||
Vāsantī: May Your Majesty please take a seat here for now; this is the hermitage of the Lord. (Rāma sits down.
Vāsantī:
This is the stone slab serving as your bed, situated in the midst of a dense grove of young plantain trees, where you rested with your beloved;
while staying here, Sītā offered even blades of grass to the wild animals, and for that reason, she was never abandoned by the deer.
Rāma:
This is impossible to behold. (He sits down elsewhere, weeping.
Sītā:

Friend Vāsantī! What have you done by showing this to me and to my noble lord? Alas, woe! It is that same noble lord; it is that same forest of Pañcavaṭī; it is that same dear friend Vāsantī; those same regions of the Godāvarī grove are witnesses to our various intimacies; and those same beasts and birds and trees are no different from when they were born. Yet for me, unfortunate as I am, though all this is visible, it does not exist. Such has become the transformation of the world of the living!
Vāsantī:
Friend Sītā! Why do you not behold the condition of the noble Rāma?
Even though he is constantly visible to us at his own will, providing a festival for the eyes with limbs as tender as fresh *kula* flowers, he remains ever new.
Though his senses are impaired, his complexion pale, and he is utterly weakened by grief, he must somehow be inferred to be him; yet even so, he is dear to my sight.
Sītā:
Friend! I see it. Tamasā:—
"Look again at my beloved!

She stood there looking, saying, "Ah, seen! "Alas, Fate! Who could have imagined that he would be without me, and I without him? Therefore, for even a single moment, let me behold my dear noble son, whose sight was difficult to obtain even in another birth, now seen amidst these tears."

Tamasā—(Embracing her, with tears) Shedding a flood of agitated tears born of both joy and sorrow, your gaze—with its long, upturned lashes—is drenching the Lord of Compassion; flowing with affection, it is as white, sweet, and charming as a stream of milk. (23)
Vāsantī: Let the trees, dripping with honey, offer an oblation of flowers and fruits; let the forest breezes blow, filled with the fragrance of blooming lotuses;
let the birds, their throats impassioned, warble sweet and continuous notes—for once again, this Lord Rāma has come to the forest in person. (24)
Rāma: Come, friend Vāsantī! Surely you should stay here.
Vāsantī: [Does so.]
(Sitting down, with tears) Great King! Is all well with Prince Lakṣmaṇa?
Rāma—(Acting as if he has not heard): Maithilī nourished the trees, the birds, and the deer with water, wild grain, and young grass offered by her lotus-like hands.
When they are seen, a certain transformation arises within me, like a liquid from a compassionate heart ready to overflow. || 25 ||
Vāsantī: Great King! Am I not asking after the welfare of Prince Lakṣmaṇa?
Rāma: [He speaks.]

(To herself) Ah! "O Great King"—what a formal address, devoid of intimacy! A question of welfare with syllables faltering due to tears, directed toward one who is merely the son of Sumitrā! From this I think that she must already know the news concerning Sītā. (Aloud) Ah! Is Prince Lakṣmaṇa well? Vāsantī—(Weeps) Oh, my Lord! How indeed can you be so cruel?
Sītā: Friend Vāsantī! Why do you speak in such a manner? My noble husband is worthy of honor by everyone, and especially by my dear friend.
Vāsantī:

"You are my life, you are my compassion; you are a second moonlight for my eyes, and you are nectar upon my limbs"—with hundreds of such endearments, he coaxed that innocent girl. Or rather, let this be; what is the use of saying more? || 26 ||
(Thus he faints.
Tamasā:
It is only fitting that his speech has ceased and he has fainted.
Rāma:
Friend! Take heart, take heart! Vāsantī:
(Recovering her breath) So, what is this improper act that has been committed by my lord?
Sītā: Friend Vāsantī! Desist, desist!
Rāma:
"The world will not tolerate it. Vāsantī: [continues]
For what reason?
Rāma:
He alone knows something.
Tamasā:
A long-awaited reproach.
Vāsantī says:

O cruel one! Fame is indeed dear to you; but is there not a far more terrible infamy than this? What happened to that fawn-eyed woman in the forest? Tell me, my lord! Alas, how can you possibly think such a thing? || 27 ||
Sītā:
Friend Vāsantī! You alone are cruel and heartless, since you cause him to prattle in this way as he is already prattling.
Tamasā:
Affection speaks thus, as does grief.
Rāma:

Friend, what is there to be considered in this matter? The creeper-like body of her—whose eyes were as tremulous as those of a frightened yearling deer, and who was languid from the weight of her throbbing womb—has surely been devoured by carnivorous beasts, appearing like soft young lotus stalks made of moonlight.
Sītā:
Noble husband! I am still alive; I am still alive.
Rāma:
Alas, my beloved Jānakī! Where are you?
Sītā:
Alas, woe! Alas, woe! My noble husband is weeping aloud as if he were someone else.
Tamasā:
Child, this is only appropriate for the present moment. Those who suffer must indeed find a way to dispel their sorrow.
When a tank overflows with water, the outlet is the remedy.
And in the agitation of grief, one is sustained only by lamentations. || 29 ||
In particular, for the noble Rāma, this world of living beings is fraught with manifold sufferings.
This entire universe must be protected with a mind diligently applied according to dharma; yet, grief for his beloved withers his life-force like a flower.
Having himself performed the act of abandonment, even the diversion of lamentation is difficult to obtain; that he still breathes even now—surely, even weeping is a gain.

Rāma: Alas, oh! Alas! My heart breaks from the agitation of grief, yet it does not split in two; my distressed body bears delusion, yet it does not lose consciousness. An internal burning consumes my frame, yet it does not reduce it to ashes; Fate strikes me down, piercing my vital organs, yet it does not cut short my life. (31)

O venerable citizens of the city and the countryside! Since your ladyship’s residence in our home was not to your liking, she was abandoned like a blade of grass in the empty forest, and yet we did not even grieve for her.
Those long-familiar impressions still move me so deeply; therefore, have mercy on us who are now without refuge, for we are weeping.
Vāsantī—(To herself) This is an exceedingly profound filling of the burden of grief. (Aloud) Your Majesty! Since it has passed, let fortitude be maintained.
Rāma—
What is called fortitude? It is this: that it is the twelfth year of the Goddess’s voiding of the world;
even the name [of Rāma] has perished as if it were non-existent, yet Rāma does not cease to live.
Sītā:
And yet, as if deluded, I am captivated by these affectionate words of my noble husband.
Tamasā: — [continues]
Even so, my child! These words, though most dear and moist with affection, are harsh with grief;
they are like streams of honey dripping upon you that are nonetheless full of poison.
Rāma:
O Vāsantī!
Indeed, it was as if a flaming brand were driven obliquely into my heart, or as if a venomous fang had been implanted within me.
In that very same way, why was the intense spike of grief not endured, even as it cut through one's vital organs? || 35 ||
Sītā:
Even so, I am ill-fated, for I am once again a source of distress to my noble husband.
Rāma: [Listens.]
Thus, even for me, whose inner heart is so deeply suppressed and stilled, this agitation has arisen today from the sight of a familiar object. For indeed:

whatever effort is somehow applied within to restrain the surging of compassion, which is turbulent like the tide, that very effort the mind’s transformation abandons and breaks through, spreading forth by force—just as the irresistible current of water overflows a sandbank dam. (36)
Sītā:
By this union with suffering, brought about by my noble husband’s irresistible and cruel resolve, my heart—its own sorrow eclipsed—is bursting, and my life is being cast away.
Vāsantī:
(To himself) Alas, the King is deeply attached. Therefore, I shall distract him for a moment. (Aloud) May Your Majesty honor these regions of Janasthāna, long familiar to you, by beholding them now.
Rāma: So be it. (Rising and walking about.)
Sītā:
I suspect that the very intensification of my sorrow is the means by which my dear friend intends to divert me.
Vāsantī:
O God of gods!
It was in this very bower that you stood, casting your gaze along her path; she, meanwhile, remained for a long time on the sands of the Godāvarī, her curiosity piqued by the swans.
Seeing you appear dejected as she approached, she, overcome with timidity, pressed her charming hands together in salutation like a lotus bud. (37)
Sītā:
You are cruel, Vāsantī! You are cruel! For you remind me, unfortunate as I am, and my noble husband again and again with these clusters of arrows that have pierced the very vitals of my heart.
Rāma:

O cruel Jānakī! You are seen here and there, yet you do not take pity on me. Alas, alas, O Queen! My heart is bursting, the bonds of my body are falling apart; I perceive the world as a void and burn with an internal flame.
Failing and distressed in blinding darkness, my inner soul seems to sink away; delusion envelops me from all sides—what can I, unfortunate as I am, do? (38)
(Thus he faints.
Sītā:
Alas, woe! Alas, woe! My noble husband has fainted once again!
Vāsantī:
My lord, take heart, take heart! Sītā: [Faints]

"Noble son! Alas, for me, unfortunate as I am, you—who have obtained birth as an auspicious blessing for the entire world of living beings—have undergone this terrible transformation of state, where your life is repeatedly placed in jeopardy! Oh, I am ruined!
Tamasā:
"Child, take heart, take heart! Once again, the touch of Rāmabhadra’s hand is the means for your survival."
Vāsantī: Why does she still not breathe? Alas, dear friend Sītā! Where are you? Show yourself to the lord of your life! Vāsantī: [continues]
"By good fortune, Rāmabhadra has regained consciousness. (Sītā approaches with agitation and touches his forehead.
Rāma:
[He speaks] as if anointing the elements of my body, both within and without, with ointments composed of nectar.

Furthermore, this touch, reviving me all of a sudden, brings about a delusion as if it were something other than joy. (With joy, eyes still closed. Friend Vāsantī! By good fortune, you are prospering.
Vāsantī: How so?
Rāma:
Friend! What else could it be? Jānakī has been found once again.
Vāsantī: [Listens.]
O Lord Rāmabhadra! Where is she?
Rāma—(acting out the pleasure of touch) Look, is she not right here before us?

Vāsantī: Oh, noble Rāmabhadra! Why do you burn me again—me, unfortunate as I am—with these ravings so cruel that they cut to the very vitals, when I am already consumed by the grief of my dear friend’s calamity?
Sītā: [Listens.]

I wish to withdraw. Yet, by the touch of my noble husband—so gentle and cool with the weight of long-standing affection, which instantly alleviates even this long-drawn agony—I find my hand, though its functions are paralyzed as if bound by adamantine glue, remains stuck fast.
Rāma:

Friend, why this delirium? This hand of mine, which was formerly grasped during the marriage ceremony while wearing the wedding bracelet, and which has been familiarized by the nectar-cool rays of the moon;

"This very hand of hers, so beautiful by comparison with her other hand, resembling a delicate sprout of the lavalī creeper, has been obtained by me. (He takes it.
Sītā: Alas, woe! Alas, woe! A lapse has occurred on my part, as I am bewildered by the touch of my noble husband.
Rāma:
Friend Vāsantī! My eyes are closed in bliss; overcome by the trepidation of my beloved’s touch, I am no longer master of myself. Therefore, you too must support me.
Vāsantī: [Supports him.]
"Alas, it is indeed madness! (Sītā, withdrawing her hand with agitation, steps back.
Rāma:

Shame! A lapse of care! That sprout-like hand of hers, suddenly falling from my own hand—which is numb and has become numb—was trembling as it fell from my trembling hand, and perspiring as it fell from my perspiring hand. (41)
Sītā:
Alas, woe! Alas, woe! Even now, with my pain still persisting and causing such violent dizziness, I cannot steady myself.
Tamasā:

(Gazing with an affectionate, curious smile) With her limbs perspiring, bristling with horripilation, and trembling, the dear child has become one through the bliss of her beloved’s touch—like a kadamba branch shaken and sprinkled by fresh rain, its buds suddenly bursting open. (42)
Sītā—(To herself) I have been made to feel ashamed by this very person against my will, by the venerable Tamasā. Why indeed will she think: "This is an abandonment; this is an insult"?
Rāma—
(Looking all around) Alas! How is it that she is truly not here? O pitiless Vaidehī!
Sītā:
I am indeed pitiless, for I continue to live even while beholding you in such a state.
Rāma:
Where are you, my beloved? O Queen, be gracious, be gracious! You ought not to abandon me in such a state.
Sītā:
Oh noble son! This is as if contrary to all reason.
Vāsantī:
My Lord, be gracious, be gracious! Restrain yourself with your own extraordinary fortitude when you have reached such an excess. Where is my dear friend?
Rāma:

Clearly, she is not here at all. Otherwise, how could even Vāsantī not see her? Could this indeed be a dream? But I am not asleep. How could Rāma sleep? In every way, it is that same divine delusion, imagined by me many times, that pursues me again and again. Sītā:
"My noble husband has been deceived by me, that cruel woman!
Vāsantī: "My Lord! Look, look!"
This iron chariot of the descendant of Pulastya has been shattered by Jaṭāyu; and here before you are those asses, their remains now mere skeletons with faces like Piśācas.
Here the enemy rises up toward the sky like a cloud containing internal lightning, carrying the moving Sītā while his own wing-joints are severed by the sword-blade of Jaṭāyu.
Sītā—(Terrified) Noble son! My father is being slain! Therefore, protect me, protect me! I too am being carried away.
Rāma—
(Rising with impetuosity) Ah, you villain! You who have stolen Sītā, the very life-breath of my father! O Lord of Laṅkā, where will you go? Vāsantī:
Oh, my Lord, you who are the comet of destruction for the race of Rākṣasas! Is there still anyone remaining to be the object of your wrath?
Sītā:
Oh! I am utterly bewildered.
Rāma:—
Now, quite another reversal has come to pass:

Through the presence of means for diversion and through the crushing conflicts of heroes that produced a most wonderful sentiment in the world, that separation from the lovely-eyed one indeed had its end in the slaying of the enemy; it was bitter, yet endured in silence. But this dissolution is endless. (44)
Sītā:
I was held in high esteem during our former separation; alas! To think it is now without end—I am ruined.
Rāma: [Listens.]
Alas, how painful it is!

Where even my friendship with the Lord of Monkeys is in vain, where the prowess of the monkeys is useless, where Jāmbavat’s wisdom fails, and where even the son of Vāyu has no way; where even Nala, the son of Viśvakarman, is unable to construct a path, and which lies beyond the range of even Lakṣmaṇa’s arrows—there, O beloved, where are you to me? || 45 ||
Sītā: I was highly honored during our former separation.
Rāma:—
Friend Vāsantī! Seeing Rāma now will only lead to further sorrow. How much longer shall I make you weep? Therefore, grant me leave to depart.
Sītā—(Embracing Tamasā with agitation and fainting) Alas, blessed Tamasā! My noble husband is departing now. What am I to do? (She faints.)
Tamasā:

Child Jānakī, take heart, take heart! Destiny will be favorable to you. Therefore, let us go to the very presence of Bhāgīrathī to perform the auspicious rites for the growth of the venerable Kuśa and Lava.
Sītā:
"O Blessed One! Be gracious; I behold you, whose sight is difficult to obtain even for a mere moment.
Rāma:
"Now, I have one who shares the religious duties of my horse-sacrifice."
Sītā—(With reproach) Noble son? Who?
Vāsantī—
"Was she even married?
Rāma: "No, no. It was a golden image of Sītā."
Sītā—(With tears and a sigh of relief) Noble son! Now you are truly my own. Oh! My thorn of abandonment has now been extracted by my noble son!
Rāma—
Even there, for now, I shall divert my eyes, which are stained with tears.
Sītā:
Truly blessed is she who is thus highly esteemed by my noble husband; truly, she who thus diverts my noble husband has become the very bond of hope for the world of the living.
Tamasā—(Embracing her with a smile moistened by affection: Oh, my child! Is this how you praise yourself?
Sītā—
(With bashfulness) I have been teased by the venerable lady.
Vāsantī:
This great matter is a favor to us; let it be arranged so that there is no neglect of our duty regarding the departure.
