Vāsantī has now become an adversary to me.
Tamasā: My child, come, let us go.
Sītā: We shall do so. Tamasā:—
Or how is it understood?
For her, whose gaze is long with longing as if sewn upon her beloved, the close proximity [of the object] is blocked by efforts resembling the cutting of one's vital organs. (46)
Sītā:
Homage to the lotus-feet of my noble husband, which are worthy of being beheld by those of well-performed merit and virtue. (She faints.
Tamasā:—
Take heart.
Sītā—
(recovering her breath) How long will your sight of the full moon remain hidden behind the clouds?
Tamasā: Oh! What a marvelous arrangement!
There is but a single aesthetic flavor, namely the pathetic (*karuṇa*); yet, through the diversity of its causes, it assumes various transformations as if it were distinct in each case.
Just as water possesses transformations consisting of whirlpools, bubbles, and waves, yet all of that is indeed only water; || 47 ||
Rāma:

O King of Vimānas! This way, this way! (All rise. Tamasā and Vāsantī (to Sītā and Rāma): The Earth, the River of the Gods, those like us, and that first patriarch of the lineages who was the original author of the Vedic meters; all these have come here to behold you.
And may that sage Vasiṣṭha, followed by Arundhatī, grant you prosperity for the sake of even greater auspiciousness. || 48 ||
(Thus they all exit.
Thus ends the third act, named "The Shadow," in the *Uttararāmacarita* composed by the great poet Bhavabhūti. || 3 ||
(Then enter two ascetics.
One:
Saudhātaki! Behold today the exceeding beauty of the venerable Vālmīki’s hermitage, made so charming by the great bustle of the many guests who have been gathered here.

For thus it is: the forest deer, having just given birth, drinks its fill of the warm, sweet scum of wild rice porridge—more delicious than that which a beloved wife has just drunk—and the fragrance of cooking vegetables mixed with jujube fruits and ghee spreads abroad, faintly followed by the scent of the cooked food.
Saudhātaki:
Welcome to you, sirs, many kinds of ascetics with worn-out beards, who provide no cause for interruption of study. First:
(Laughing) Saudhātaki, the reason for this unprecedented high esteem toward elders is indeed remarkable!
Saudhātaki:
O Daṇḍāyana! What is the name of this leader of a great caravan of women who has arrived today as our guest?
Daṇḍāyana:

Fie on this mockery! Is it not true that the venerable Vasiṣṭha has arrived from the hermitage of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, bringing Arundhatī with him, to attend upon the wives of the great king Daśaratha? Why then do you prattle thus?
Saudhātaki:
Hm, Vasiṣṭha?
Daṇḍāyana:
Indeed so?
Saudhātaki: Yes.
"But I have realized that this man is like some tiger.
Daṇḍāyana: "Ah! What do you mean by that?"
Saudhātaki: By that very person who has arrived, that poor, auspicious Kapilā cow was forcibly made to low "maḍamaḍā.
Daṇḍāyana:

Householders, highly respecting the traditional injunction that the *madhuparka* offering must include meat, slaughter a heifer or a great bull for a learned guest who has arrived; for the authors of the *Dharma-sūtras* prescribe that as the law.
Saudhātaki:
O sir! You are caught!
Daṇḍāyana: [He speaks.]
"How so?
Saudhātaki:

"Because when the venerable Vasiṣṭha and his company arrived, the heifer was slaughtered. But for the royal sage Janaka, who has returned this very day, the blessed Vālmīki prepared the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) with only curds and honey; furthermore, the heifer was released."
Daṇḍāyana:
Some declare this to be the rule for those who have not desisted from meat; however, the honorable Janaka has desisted from meat.
Saudhātaki:
"What is the cause?
Daṇḍāyana replied:

"Having heard of such a misfortune of fate befalling Queen Sītā, that ascetic became a forest-dweller; it has been several years since he has been performing austerities in the penance grove on Candradvīpa."
Saudhātaki:
What happened after that? Daṇḍāyana: [He] arrived.
And now, I wish to see the venerable Prācetas, the beloved of Sudarśana.
Saudhātaki:
Has he not already had an audience with Rāma today through his kinswomen?
Daṇḍāyana:
Just now the venerable Vasiṣṭha has sent the lady Arundhatī to Queen Kausalyā, saying, "She must go in person out of affection to see her.
Saudhātaki: [Listens.]

"Just as these elders have gathered together with one another, so shall we two also gather with the young students and honor the great festival of the suspension of studies by sporting. Now, where is that Janaka?
Daṇḍāyana:
"In this manner, having paid his respects to Vālmīki and Vasiṣṭha, he is now seated at the foot of a tree outside the hermitage. He is this very person here."
He is tormented by the grief for Sītā, which is ever-present in his heart,
like an ancient tree with fire creeping within it.
(Thus they both exit. This concludes the mixed interlude.
(Then Janaka enters. Janaka:

Because of that great calamity which befell my offspring—a calamity that clings to me with its intense sting, wounding my heart and causing it agony—my grief does not cease; sharp, continuous, and as fresh as ever, it cuts through my vital organs like a saw. (3)

Alas! Even though my internal bodily constituents have been withered by old age, by insurmountable suffering, and further by austerities such as the *parāka* and *sāntapana*, there is still support! My burnt body has not yet fallen even into the great river. "For those worlds called *andhatāmisra* and *asurya*, which are devoid of sunlight, are ordained after death for those who commit suicide"—thus the sages believe.

Even after the passing of many years, this terrible surge of suffering does not subside for me; though it is fresh, its appearance remains vivid through moment-by-moment contemplation. O Mother, born from the sacrificial ground of the gods! Such is the portion of your creation that has now ripened, that even out of shame one cannot cry aloud at will. Alas, my daughter! I remember your lotus-face as an infant—with its unpredictable tears and smiles, its few shining, tender buds of teeth, and your charming, faltering, and incoherent prattle.
O Blessed Vasundharā! You are truly of most firm resolve.

You are the fire, you are the sages, you are the wife of Vasiṣṭha, and you are the Gaṅgā; if even the Sun himself, the divine preceptor of Raghu’s lineage, knows your majesty—just as Speech gave birth to Knowledge—then why, O cruel one, do you tolerate the execution of that very daughter of yours who has attained such purity? (6)

(Offstage) This way, this way, O venerable ones, great queens! Janaka: Ah! Is it the venerable Arundhatī, whose path is being shown by Gṛṣṭi? (Rising) But which "great queen" does he say she is? (Looking closely) Alas, alas! How is this Kausalyā—the lawful wife of the great king Daśaratha and my dear friend? Who could believe that she is indeed this very person? She dwelt in the house of Daśaratha like the Goddess Śrī herself; what further comparison is needed for her? She is Śrī herself.
Alas, by the power of fate, something else entirely has arisen—a certain being consisting of suffering; oh, what a transformation!
Those very people who were previously my embodied great festival have become as unbearable to behold as salt upon a wound. (7)
(Then enter Arundhatī, Kausalyā, and the Chamberlain.
Arundhatī:

Indeed, I told you that "the King of Videha must be seen by going to him in person"—such was the command of your family preceptor. It was for this very reason that I was sent. So why is there this great hesitation at every step?
Chamberlain: My Queen, compose yourself and comply with the command of the venerable Vasiṣṭha; this is what I report to you.
Kausalyā: [Listens.]

"At such a time as this, the thought 'the Lord of Mithilā must be seen by me' causes all sorrows to descend upon one simultaneously. Therefore, I am unable to steady my heart, whose root-bonds are being torn asunder. Arundhatī:
"What doubt is there in this?
Even for human beings, sorrows arising from separation from kinsmen flow in an unbroken stream."
Upon seeing a beloved person, unbearable sorrows flood forth as if by thousands of streams. ||8||
Kausalyā: How indeed shall we show the face of my dear daughter-in-law, who has gone to the forest, to her father, that royal seer?
Arundhatī:
This is your praiseworthy kinsman, the upholder of the Janaka lineage,
to whom the sage Yājñavalkya sang the complete study of the Veda (Brahmapārāyaṇa).

Kausalyā: This is that King of Videha, Sīradhvaja, who was no different from a father to my dear husband, the Great King. I am reminded of those days, delightful in their freedom from sorrow. (Approaching) Venerable Arundhatī! Sīradhvaja of Videha greets you.
She by whom even the ocean—though already considered pure—is purified, she who is the Lord of the holy luster, and indeed the greatest of all teachers, even of the ancient seers;
her, the Goddess who is auspicious to the three worlds and worthy of the world’s worship, I salute with my head bowed to the ground, as one salutes the divine Dawn. (10)
Arundhatī:
May that imperishable light of yours shine forth! May that supreme deity who blazes beyond the realms of space purify you.
Janaka: [Listens.]

"Noble Gṛṣṭi! Is all well with this mother of the protector of the people? Chamberlain: (Welcoming him) We have been reproached most thoroughly and excessively. (Aloud) O Royal Sage! You ought not, by means of this very same indignation, to cause further pain to the Queen, who is already deeply distressed and has long been deprived of the sight of Prince Rāmabhadra. There is also some ill fortune of fate regarding Rāmabhadra himself; for the citizens are spreading loathsome rumors on all sides, and since the majority do not accept the purification by fire, Your Majesty has acted most cruelly.

Janaka—(With anger) Ah! Who is this so-called fire for purifying our offspring? Alas! While people speak thus, we are being insulted once again, even though we have already been insulted by the noble Rāma.
Arundhatī—
(Sighing) It is even so. "Fire" are but light syllables when addressed to my child; "Sītā" alone is sufficient. Alas, my child!
Whether you are a child or a disciple—let that be as it may—yet the excellence of your purity strengthens my fear for you.
Be it childhood or femininity, you are indeed worthy of homage by the worlds; among those possessed of virtue, it is virtues that are the object of worship, neither gender nor age. (11)
Kausalyā: Alas! These pains seem to be uprooting me entirely. (She faints.
Janaka:
Ah! What is this?
Arundhatī—O royal sage, what else could it be?
That king, that happiness, those children, and those days—all of it has appeared within your memory now that you are clearly seen.
Indeed, your friend was not at all deluded during this terrible calamity; for the hearts of housewives are as delicate as flowers. (12)
Janaka:
Alas! I am altogether cruel, since I look upon my dear daughter-in-law and my beloved wife, whom I have not seen for so long, as if I were indifferent to them.
That kinsman is praiseworthy; those two dear daughters-in-law and that couple, that very joy—even in person—is the entire fruit of life.

Was there nothing, O Great King, dearer to me than my own body or life, that the illustrious Daśaratha was not so to me? Alas, this is indeed Kausalyā— that I became the object of reproach for both husband and wife, as if I had been privily plotting against her lord.
Thereafter, fate became entirely subservient to his will, whether in bestowing favor or in wrath; for remembering that [past conduct], it burns him by violently leaping upon his compassion.
Arundhatī: Alas! How painful! Her heart has become motionless due to her sighs being suppressed for so long.
Janaka: [He faints.]
"Alas, dear friend! (With these words, she sprinkles her with water from her water-pot. Chamberlain:
Having first displayed a favorable disposition that was singularly consistent and bestowed happiness, Fate now leaves behind only the pain of the heart, cruel as its sudden reversal. (15)

Kausalyā—(Recovering her breath) Alas, my child Jānaki! Where are you? I remember your lotus-face, so blooming and lovely, which was the sole auspicious sign upon receiving the splendor of your new marriage, and which was as beautiful as the rising moonlight. Come back to me, my daughter; once again illumine my lap. The Great King always used to say: "She is the bride of the elders of the Raghu clan, yet to us she is simply Janaka’s daughter, our own child. Chamberlain—
As the Queen said: "Even among his five sons, Subāhuśatru was especially dear to that king;
likewise, even among his four daughters-in-law, no other daughter-in-law was as beloved to him as Sītā. (16)
Janaka:

Alas, dear friend, Great King Daśaratha! You were so compassionate toward everyone in every way; how can you be forgotten? It is said that fathers honor the trusted kinsmen of their daughter’s husband; yet in this alliance, your service toward me was quite the opposite.
Though you were such a person, you have fallen at this time; and that seed of our relationship has been cast into this terrible hell of my world of the living—fie on the life of a sinner!
Kausalyā: My child Jānaki! What shall I do? This wretched life of mine, rendered motionless by the firm obstruction of adamantine cement, will not abandon me, unfortunate as I am.
Arundhatī: [She speaks.]

"Take heart, O Queen! Even a respite from your tears must surely be taken at intervals. Moreover, do you not remember what your family preceptor said in the hermitage of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga: 'It was destined to happen thus; it has indeed come to pass. However, its outcome shall be auspicious.
Kausalyā:
(How can this be for me, whose desires have been so utterly frustrated?)"
Arundhatī:
What do you think, O Queen? Is that a falsehood? Indeed, O Kṣatriya lady, you must not think so.
Let there be no doubt regarding the utterances of Brāhmaṇas whose inner light has become manifest.
For auspicious fortune is firmly fixed in their speech; they do not utter words whose meaning is corrupted. ||18||
(A confused noise behind the scenes; everyone listens.
Janaka:
Ah, this is the clamor of schoolboys playing without restraint because it is not a day for study.

Kausalyā: Childhood is now a time when happiness is easily attained. Oh! Who among these is this boy who cools our eyes with limbs that are charmingly playful, supported by the youthful splendor of the noble Rāma? Arundhatī:

(To himself, with joy and longing) This is indeed the secret nectar for my ears, revealed by Bhāgīrathī; yet I do not know which of the two long-lived ones, Kuśa or Lava, this may be. (Aloud) With locks of hair as dark and glossy as blue lotus petals, adorned with a topknot, and possessing a merit-filled splendor that honors the assembly of young students with its very beauty—is this my dear Raghunandana, returned to childhood, who, upon being seen, suddenly acts as a salve of nectar for my eyes? Who is he? (19)
Chamberlain: I believe this boy must surely be a Kṣatriya student (brahmacārin).
Janaka: [Listens.]

Now this army stands motionless as if painted; surely the Jṛmbhakāstra, whose power is invincible, is yawning forth.
A marvel, a marvel! The sky is overspread by the *Jṛmbhakas*, dark as the thick darkness massed within the caverns of the underworld, blazing with the glowing, tawny radiance of molten gold;

they are like the peaks of the Vindhya mountains, which, when cast down by the fierce and terrible winds that bring about the end of an aeon, have their hollows reddened by lightning amidst the clouds of rainwater.
Sumantra:
But from where could he have obtained these Jṛmbhakas?
Candraketu:
"We believe it was from the Blessed One Prācetasa.
Sumantra:
"Child, it is not so; especially regarding weapons, and particularly the Jṛmbhakas, for—"
For these are the sons of Kṛśāśva; from Kṛśāśva they passed to Kauśika, and then, through that tradition, they came to reside in Rāmabhadra. || 15 ||
Candraketu:
Others as well, whose light of inner being is increasing, see everything for themselves through the vision of mantra.
Sumantra: [He continues.]
Child! Be on your guard; your rival warrior has arrived. The two princes—(to each other):
Oh! What a handsome youth this prince is! (Gazing at him with affectionate longing.)
Is this a chance encounter? Or perhaps an excellence of my multitude of virtues? Or is it an ancient acquaintance formed through the dense bonds of previous births?
Or is it some unknown innate relationship? Whatever it may be by the power of fate, upon seeing him, he bestows this compassionate attention upon me. (16)
Sumantra:

This is the nature of the majority of living beings; therein, the affection of some for another arises spontaneously, which worldly people describe as "friendship with the stars" or "love at first sight. They declare that this has an incalculable cause. There is no remedy for that partiality which is without a [discernible] cause; for it is a thread of affection that sews together all internal beings. (17)

The two princes—(addressing each other): How could arrows be discharged against their bodies, which are as smooth as royal sandalwood paste, and upon reaching which my limbs remain with their hair standing on end from the desire to embrace them? (18)
Moreover, when one has been confronted by such fierce splendor, what recourse is there indeed other than a weapon? Yet, what can even that weapon achieve against one whose nature is such as this?
What will he himself say if I turn away from battle even while my weapon is raised? For the code of heroes is of a cruel spirit; it obstructs the course of affection. (19)

Sumantra—(Gazing at Lava, with tears, to himself) Alas! Why do you flutter so aimlessly? That which was the seed of my desire has been destroyed by fate from the very beginning. When the creeper has already been cut down, how can there be the emergence of fruit? || 20 ||
Candraketu:
Noble Sumantra, let us descend from the chariot.
Sumantra: [Does so.]
For what reason?
Candraketu:

On one hand, this heroic man is honored; moreover, O Noble One, the duty of the Kṣatriya is preserved! Those learned in the scriptures declare: "Chariot-warriors do not attack one who travels on foot."
Sumantra—(To himself) Ah! I have fallen into a miserable state.
For how could one such as I possibly forbid this course of action?
Or how could he possibly sanction an action whose sole essence is rashness? || 21 ||
Candraketu:
Since even my venerable father asks you, his dear friend, regarding matters of doubt, why does your honor hesitate?
Sumantra:
"O long-lived one! It is indeed as you consider it to be according to dharma. This is the rule for battle; this is the eternal dharma.
For this is the path of heroic conduct followed by the lions of the Raghu dynasty. (22)
Candraketu:
Your noble words are incomparable.
[For] history, the Purāṇas, and the expositions on Dharma—
You yourselves know the established tradition of the Raghu dynasty. || 23 ||
Sumantra:
(Embracing him with tears of affection) My child, my dear child! How many days indeed have passed since you were born, you who are the slayer even of your father’s enemy, Indrajit?
His offspring, too, shall follow the dharma of heroes; by good fortune, the lineage of Daśaratha has attained its firm foundation.
Candraketu— (with distress):
"If the eldest of the lineage has no standing, what standing can our family have?"
Thus our three other ancestors suffer from this misery. (25)
Sumantra:
These words of Candraketu are indeed piercing the very vitals of my heart. Lava: [Listens.]
Ah! A sentiment of mingled emotions prevails.
Just as the night-lily rejoices when the moon has risen, so does my gaze toward him; yet this one is desirous of strife.
His arm—bearing love for his great bow that resounds with the harsh twang of its vibrating string—is marked by gaping and formidable wounds. (26)
Candraketu—(Observing his descent) Noble sir! This is that Candraketu, descendant of Ikṣvāku, who greets you.
Sumantra—

May the Great Primeval Boar bring about the utter defeat of that which is harmful. Furthermore, may the divine Savitṛ inspire you; may he who is the lord of your lineage, the son of Mitra and Varuṇa, rejoice in you—he who is the teacher even of teachers.
May there be for you the power of Indra, Viṣṇu, Agni, the Maruts, and Suparṇa; and may the mantra-like sound of the bowstring of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa grant you victory.
Lava:
Indeed, he looks most splendid while standing upon his chariot. Enough, enough with such excessive courtesy.
Candraketu:
"In that case, let the illustrious one also adorn another chariot.
Lava: "Noble sir, place the prince back upon the chariot!"
Sumantra:
You too should comply with the words of my dear child Candraketu. Lava: [Listens.]
What consideration can there be for one's own belongings? But we are forest-dwellers, unpracticed in the management of chariots.
Sumantra:
You know, my child, how pride and nobility act. If King Rāmabhadra of the Ikṣvāku line were to see you in such a state, his affection would overflow with compassion for you.
Lava:

And furthermore, Candraketu! That royal sage is renowned as a virtuous man. (As if with modesty) If even we are such enemies of the foes of sacrifice, who would not hold that king in high esteem for his virtues?
Indeed, even that speech of mine caused agitation among the horse-keepers because of its fierce intensity in challenging all the warriors.
Candraketu:
Is it that you feel indignation even at the excellence of your father’s majesty? Lava: [He speaks.]

Let there be no resentment here, or let it not be so; I ask this other thing: we hear that King Rāghava is self-controlled; he indeed does not pride himself, nor do his subjects become arrogant. So why do men utter such demonic speech toward him?
The seers say that demonic speech belongs to the insane and the arrogant;
it is the source of all enmities, for it is the ruin of the world. (29)
Thus they used to censure that [other] speech and praise this one:
"It milks desire at will, it drives away misfortune, it gives birth to fame, and it bestows nourishment.
The wise call pure, peaceful, auspicious, and true speech the mother of blessings and the cow. (30)
Sumantra:
Alas, this prince, the disciple of Vālmīki, has been insulted; he speaks with an impulse of indignation that has been aroused. Lava:—

Furthermore, O Candraketu, as for what you say—“Why do you feel indignation even at the excellence of your father’s prowess?”—I ask this: “Is the duty of a warrior (*kṣatradharma*) restricted to a specific domain?
Sumantra:
Indeed, you do not know the divine descendant of Ikṣvāku! Therefore, desist from this excessive persistence.
By crushing the soldiers, you have truly displayed your prowess;
however, you ought not to persist in the subduing of the son of Jamadagni.
Lava: (With a laugh) Noble sir! What is this loud talk about that king being the subduer of Jamadagni’s son?

For it is established that the twice-born possess valor in speech, while the valor of kṣatriyas lies in their arms. Since the Brāhmaṇa Jamadagni was one who took up the sword, what praise can there be for that king in having subdued him? || 32 ||

Candraketu—(As if with agitation) Noble Sumantra! Enough of further inquiry. This is some new incarnation of a hero, even for whom the venerable descendant of Bhṛgu is no match; he who does not even know of your father’s meritorious deeds, which served as the sacrificial fee of granting safety to the seven worlds.
Lava:

Who indeed does not know the deeds and the greatness of the Lord of the Raghus? If there is indeed something that must be said—well then, let it be. Let those elders remain, whose conduct is beyond reproach; for they are great men in this world, their fame unimpeded even in the slaying of Sunda’s wife.
Even those three steps taken toward the battlefield of Khara were skillful; indeed, people are well aware of his proficiency even in the slaying of Indra’s son.
Candraketu:
Ah, you reviler of my father! You breaker of bounds! You truly act with excessive insolence! Lava:
Ah! He has turned his face toward me with a frown.
Sumantra: Their throbbing indicates anger; for indeed—

With his mass of hair disheveled and tossed by anger, a trembling arises throughout his entire body; his eyes, resembling the petals of a slightly blooming red lotus, turn crimson of their own accord;
and this face of his bears a beauty that surpasses both the moon with its prominent mark and the lotus with its wandering bee, through the parted curve of his eyebrows. (35)

Lava: Prince! Prince! Come, come! Let us descend to ground suitable for combat. (Thus they all exit. Thus ends the fifth act, titled "The Valor of the Princes," in the *Uttararāmacarita* composed by the great poet Bhavabhūti.
(Then enters a radiant pair of Vidyādharas in a celestial chariot.
Vidyādhara:

Oh, how truly marvelous are the heroic exploits of this pair of princes from the lineage of Vikartana, who are fierce in their sudden onset of battle and have illuminated the splendor of the Kṣatriya order—exploits that have utterly bewildered the gods and asuras! Behold, my dear, look!

As the two heroes discharge arrows incessantly, stretching their bows—which produce a terrifying clamor from the jingling of bracelets and the tinkling of small bells, and from the loud twanging of heavy bowstrings—a wondrous battle proceeds, terrifying to the world. || 1 ||
And for the sake of the two of them, a wonderful and auspicious yawn occurred, sounding like the deep roar of thunder from a great drum.

Let there fall upon these two heroes a continuous and dense shower of flowers—beautiful with clusters of blossoming golden lotuses joined together, and lovely like the nectar from the multitude of young gem-like buds of the celestial trees.
Vidyādharī:
Why has the sky before us suddenly become as difficult to behold as it were another, flashing with streaks of lightning more terrible than before?
Ādhāra:
What indeed could this be today? Is it the city situated upon the forehead of the Blue-and-Red One (Śiva), blazing with the light of the sun whirling within the lathe of Tvaṣṭṛ? (3)
(Reflecting) Ah, I understand! Prince Candraketu, overcome with agitation, has discharged an incomparable fiery weapon (*āgneya-astra*), for this descent of arrows is like fire itself. For now:
The circles of celestial chariots have indeed departed, their banners and yak-tail fans scorched and singed;
the flame, possessing the shimmering luster of fresh *kiṃśuka* flowers, consumes this fringe of the silken banners. (4)

How wonderful! Here indeed has come the divine Uṣarbudha (Fire), terrifying with his mass of blazing, flickering, and tumultuous flames, heavy with sparks crackling loudly as they burst forth like fierce fragments of thunderbolts; and his onset is violent on all sides. Therefore, covering my beloved with her garment, I shall retreat to a great distance. (She does so.

Vidyādharī: By good fortune, through this touch of my lord’s body—cool, smooth, soft, and full like a mountain of pure pearls—the heat within me has been interrupted even as it was half-arisen, for my pain is now reeling, overwhelmed by bliss.
Vidyādhara:
Ah! What have I done here? Or rather:
even without doing anything at all, one dispels sorrows through joys.
For whatever person is dear to someone, that indeed is a certain kind of substance for them.
Vidyādharī:

How is it that the courtyard of the sky is being overspread by clouds, dark as the throat of a rutting peacock and thick with the playful movements of dense, flickering, and quivering streaks of lightning?
Vidyādhara:
This is indeed the power of the Vāruṇa weapon employed by Kumāralava! How is it that the fire-weapon has been completely extinguished by the falling showers of incessant streams of water?
Vidyādharī: It is pleasing to me, it is pleasing to me!

Vidyādhara: Alas, sir! Everything in excess leads to disaster. For when a being perishes—hemmed in by a dense darkness thickened by clouds rumbling with a deep *gulugulā* sound, stirred up by the winds of universal dissolution; as if revolving within the cavernous mouth of Time, hideous and formidable as it swallows the universe all at once; with all its exits blocked by the yogic sleep of the end of the age; as if entered into the belly of Nārāyaṇa—it is truly lost. Well done, Candraketu! Well done! The Vāyavya weapon was well-aimed. For: By the wind, which is like a magical power (*vidyā*), even though there are many clouds...
Just as in Brahman, the dissolution of all transformations has been effected somewhere.
Vidyādharī:

My Lord! Who is this who now, with such haste, having raised his upper garment as it flutters from his uplifted hand, and having forbidden the act of combat with sweet and affectionate words, causes a magnificent celestial chariot to descend between these two?
Vidyādhara:—
(Seeing him) Here is the Lord of the Raghus, returned from the slaying of Śambūka.
Having heard those words spoken by the Great Man, Lava has ceased his combat out of respect for him;
Candraketu too bows down. May there be prosperity for the King through this reunion with his sons. (7)
Therefore, come this way for now. (Exeunt both. Interlude.
(Then enter Rāma, Lava, and the prostrate Candraketu.
Rāma:
(Descending from the Puṣpaka chariot: O moon of the solar dynasty! O Candraketu! Come quickly and embrace me firmly;
let the burning of my heart be extinguished by your limbs, cool as fragments of snow. (8)
(Raising him up and embracing him with tears of affection) Is all well with you, who have engaged in combat with new celestial weapons?
Candraketu:

I offer my salutations. All is well through the auspicious acquisition of this most wonderful and dear friend. Therefore, I request that my father look upon this hero, who possesses tireless courage, with an especially affectionate eye, as he would look upon me.
Rāma—(Observing Lava) By good fortune, this friend of my child possesses a form that is exceedingly profound, sweet, and auspicious.

He appears like the science of weapons incarnate, having matured in order to protect the worlds; or like the duty of the warrior class (*kṣātradharma*) embodied, having taken on a physical form for the sake of guarding the treasury of sacred knowledge (*brahmakośa*).
He was like a collection of powers, or an accumulation of virtues, appearing as if he were a mass of the world’s merit brought into manifestation. ||9||
Lava—(To himself) Oh! This great soul is visible through the power of his merit;
he is like a breath of relief for devotees, a singular and vast sanctuary.
He was like the grace of supreme Dharma, beautiful in embodied form. ||10||
How wonderful!
All opposition has ceased; a rasa thick with bliss flows forth; that former agitation vanishes somewhere, and humility bows me down.
Why am I so suddenly under its sway upon seeing him? Or rather, for the great, as for sacred pilgrimage sites, there is indeed some ineffable excellence. (11)
Rāma:

So why does this person grant me a respite from sorrow at this very moment and, for some unknown reason, win over my inner soul? Or rather, it is a contradiction to say that "affection depends upon a cause. Indeed, some internal cause interweaves all things; affections do not rely upon external conditions. For the white lotus blossoms at the rising of the sun, and the moonstone melts when the cool-rayed moon has ascended. (12)
Lava: Candraketu! Who are these?
Candraketu: [He speaks.]
"Dear friend! Are they not my father’s feet? Lava:

"To me, too, they are so by right, since you have addressed them as 'dear friend. However, there are indeed four venerable figures in the narrative of the *Rāmāyaṇa* who share such a designation. Tell me which one specifically you mean."
Candraketu:
Know me as "Elder Brother. Lava: [listens.]

(With joy) What! Is it Raghunātha himself? By good fortune, today has dawned auspiciously, since this lord has been seen! (Gazing at him with humility) Father! Lava, the disciple of Pracetasa, salutes you.
Rāma:
Long-lived one! Come, come! (Embracing him affectionately) Oh, my child! Enough of such excessive modesty. Embrace me firmly with your limbs.
Your touch—thick, smooth, and delicate like the inner petal of a fully ripened lotus, and cool as the oozing of moonlight and sandalwood—brings you joy. (13)
Lava—(To himself) Such is their causeless affection toward me! Yet, out of ignorance, I have taken up arms against them. (Aloud) May my father’s feet now forgive Lava’s childishness.
Rāma—
"What offense has the dear boy committed?
Candraketu replied, "Having heard from the horse-attendants the manifestation of my father's prowess, he has acted like a hero."
Rāma:
Indeed, this is the ornament of a Kṣatriya.
One who possesses splendor cannot endure the splendor of others when it is directed toward him. That is his innate nature; being fixed by his very constitution, it is unartificial.
If the divine Sun-god scorches unceasingly with his rays, does the stone of fire, as if insulted, vomit forth its splendors? ||14||
Candraketu:
Even his indignation befits this great hero. Behold, O venerable father! By employing the Jṛmbhaka weapon at the command of my dear friend, he has displayed his prowess and paralyzed the entire army.
Rāma:

(Staring with wonder and distress; to himself) Oh! Such is the power of my dear child? (Aloud) My child! Withdraw your weapon! And you too, Candraketu! Console the troops who are embarrassed by their lack of action. (Lava mimes concentration. Candraketu:
As instructed, [he exits].
Lava: Father! The weapon has been pacified!
Rāma:
By good fortune, the *jṛmbhaka* weapons, along with their secret methods of employment and withdrawal, have been acquired by my dear child as well.
Brahmā and the other gods, for the sake of the welfare of the Veda, performed austerities for more than a thousand years.
The ancient teachers beheld these as their own very splendors, consisting of ascetic power.

Now, the venerable Kṛśāśva imparted this secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the weapon-mantras to his disciple Kauśika, who was devoted to serving him for more than a thousand years. That venerable one [imparted it] to me; such is the lineage of gurus. I ask: from where did Kumāra receive this tradition? Lava:
Our weapons are self-luminous.
Rāma—(Reflecting) Why should it not be possible? There may be some greatness resulting from exceptionally meritorious causes. But how can there be a dual number [for the name]?
Lava—
"We two are the twin brothers!
Rāma:
"In that case, where is the second one? (Behind the scenes: "Daṇḍāyana!"
"Did you not say that the venerable Lava has indeed engaged in battle with the king's armies? Friend, it is so.
Today let the title 'King' perish throughout the worlds, and today let the flames of the weapons of the Kṣatriyas be extinguished. (16)
Rāma:

Now, who is this, possessing a luster as dark as a sapphire, who by his mere sound causes my hair to stand on end, creating a spectacle like that of the *kadamba* tree putting forth buds at the moment of the deep thundering of a fresh blue rain-cloud? (17)
Lava: This is my elder noble brother named Kuśa, who has returned from Bharata’s hermitage.
Rāma: [Observes him]...
(With curiosity) Then, my dear child! Summon that long-lived one from right here.
Lava: As you command. (He exits. (Then enters Kuśa.)

Kuśa—(Stringing his bow with indignation and composure): If there is a conflict with the Solar kings, those descendants of the Lord Vaivasvata Manu who bestowed the gift of fearlessness upon Indra and kindled the fire of their own kṣatriya prowess to subdue the arrogant, then blessed indeed is this bow of mine, its string consecrated by the fierce, flickering rays of my blazing weapons! 18.
(Walking about with a majestic stride) Rāma:
There is some extraordinary prowess in this young Kṣatriya; for instance:

With a gaze that treats the essence of all beings in the three worlds as mere straw, his steady and haughty gait seems to bend the very earth; possessing a weightiness like a mountain even in his youth, is this the heroic sentiment (vīra-rasa), or is it pride itself?
Lava—
(Approaching) Victory to the Noble One!
Kuśa—
"Indeed, long-lived one, what is this talk of 'war, war'? Lava:
"This is of little consequence. Let my noble brother, however, cast aside his pride and conduct himself with humility."
Kuśa: For what purpose? Lava:
That the Lord, the joy of the Raghus, is present here—he who is the protagonist of the *Rāmāyaṇa* stories and the guardian of the treasury of Brahman—[is indeed wonderful].

Kuśa: That great soul is one whose auspicious sight is to be longed for; however, I am deliberating upon how we should approach him. Lava: [He continues: *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with Lava's speech marker. The translation reflects the portion given.*
Just as [one behaves] toward a guru, so too by approaching him.
Kuśa: How indeed can this be so?
Lava:
The noble and most exalted Chandraketu, son of Urmilā, approaches me as a dear friend; by that relationship, according to dharma, he is indeed my father, this royal sage. Kuśa: [Silence]
Even toward a kṣatriya, humility is currently beyond reproach. (Both walk about.
Lava:
Let the noble one behold this great man, in whom various superhuman excellences of virtuous conduct are inferred by his physical form, majesty, and profundity.
Kuśa:
(Gazing) Oh, how pleasing is this form, and how purifying is this majesty!
It is only fitting that the poet of the Rāmāyaṇa has caused the Goddess of Speech to flourish. (20)
(Approaching) Father! Kuśa, the disciple of Vālmīki, salutes you.
Rāma:
Come, come, long-lived one!
Out of affection, these people long for an embrace from you, whose firm body is as smooth as a cloud filled with nectar.

(Embracing him; to himself) What is this? This boy is like the very essence of my own body, born of affection, which has flowed from limb to limb and now stands manifest outside as a single substratum of consciousness.
Drenched by the outpouring of my heart, agitated by intense bliss, this firm embrace seems to promise me a shower of snow.
Lava: The sun, scorching the forehead, is blazing hot. Therefore, let my father take a seat for a moment in the shade of this *sāla* tree.
Rāma: [Consents.]
"Whatever pleases my child. (All walk about and sit down as is appropriate.
Rāma—(to himself)
Oh! Even in their humble demeanor, the gestures, postures, and movements of both Kuśa and Lava proclaim their imperial sovereignty.
The playful manifestations of Lakṣmī, which are inseparably established within his form, manifest a loveliness that is beautiful at every moment;
just as rays belong to the stainless moon, or as drops of nectar belong to a blossomed lotus. || 24 ||
And I perceive in these two most clearly the childhood of the Raghu dynasty:

their bodies are dark like the neck of a mature pigeon, their shoulders are well-knit with the brawny humps of bulls, their gaze is steady like that of a calm lion, and their voice is as resonant as an auspicious drum. (25)

(Examining closely) Ah! Not only does her form correspond to our own lineage, but here in this pair of children there are various traits clearly resembling those of Janaka’s daughter, which can be discerned by one with keen insight.
Indeed, it is as if that face of my beloved, possessing the splendor of a fresh hundred-petaled lotus, has once again come within the range of my eyes.
This very seal of lips, beautiful with the luster of white, pure teeth, and that same curve of the ear;

Although her eyes are red and blue, nevertheless, that same quality of beauty remains. (Reflecting) This is that very forest inhabited by Vālmīki, where it is said the Queen was abandoned; for such are the physical forms, ages, and dignities of these two, and they possess weapons that are self-luminous. Even so, I remember that authorization regarding the weapons which occurred incidentally during the viewing of the paintings; perhaps that has now awakened in them. For we have never heard of weapons belonging even to the ancients that were not handed down through traditional instruction.

This is a deception of my compassionate self, wherein an excess of pleasure and pain overwhelms me with wonder; and the frequent thought that "these are twins" is merely a self-delusion. For the Queen’s state of pregnancy was marked by two signs of life (as he says through tears): "The knot of the womb, having reached its ultimate limit through the expansion of familiarity in affection, was first perceived by me alone through the skill of a touch of my palm, even though she—whose eyes were dulled by natural modesty—was confident in her privacy; thereafter, it was discovered by her after some days. (28)
(Weeping) Shall I, then, ask these two by some stratagem?
Lava: Father!
What is this? The face of you, the auspiciousness of the world, has been reduced by Bāṣparṣi to the beauty of a lotus sprinkled with dew. 29.
Kuśa:
O child! Without Queen Sītā, what indeed is not a source of sorrow for the Lord of the Raghus? For when one's beloved is lost, the entire world truly becomes a wilderness.
That affection is indeed such, yet this separation is likewise boundless; why do you ask this, as if you have not mastered the Rāmāyaṇa?

Rāma—(To himself) Ah, this conversation is neutral. Enough with questioning. O you of innocent heart! What is this sudden impulse toward compassion on your part? Thus, with the surge of my pity revealed, I am even pitied by these children. Very well, I shall withdraw for now. (Aloud) My dear ones, it is said that the *Rāmāyaṇa* is the outpouring of the Goddess Sarasvatī from the venerable Vālmīki, a panegyric of the Solar dynasty; out of curiosity, I wish to hear something of it.
Kuśa—
The entire composition has been recited by us; however, for the sake of refreshing our memory, here are these two verses concerning the childhood deeds of the boy. Rāma: Speak, my children.
Kuśa said:
"Sītā was indeed Rāma’s beloved wife, given to him by his father; moreover, their affection increased even further through her virtues and the excellence of her beauty. (31)
In the same way, Rāma became dearer to Sītā than even her own life;
indeed, he understood their mutual bond of affection.
Rāma:

Alas! What a most cruel piercing of the vitals of my heart! O Queen! Indeed, such was this [life]! Oh, how the events of worldly existence culminate in memories of deceptive separation through total and sudden reversal! Where is that joy, so abundant with unsurpassed confidence?
And where is our mutual love? And indeed, where are those profound sentiments of curiosity?
Whether in happiness or in suffering, where indeed is there any unity between the two? Nevertheless, this life-force throbs; yet the sinner does not desist. || 33 ||
Alas, what misery! That very same unbearable time, which was intent on gradually unfolding the thousands of virtues of my beloved, has now brought those very virtues back to our memory.
Then, after only a few days during which she had taken but the slightest steps, those two budding breasts of the deer-eyed girl became expansive;
therein, the activity of Love—dense with the intermingling of youth, passion, and intention—manifested both its boldness and its charm upon her body. (35)

Lava: But this verse of the Lord of the Raghus, addressed to Queen Sītā during their recreation by the Mandākinī on the path to Citrakūṭa, was composed as if for your sake: "This long stone slab has been set down here as if for your purpose."
Around which this Bakula tree seems to have rained down flowers on all sides. || 36 ||

Rāma:—(With a bashful smile, affection, and pathos) Truly, children are very simple-minded, especially those who dwell in the forest. Alas, my Queen! Do you remember that excess of intimacy during that time? Is not remembered that face—its moon-like luster upon the forehead disarrayed by locks of hair stirred by the slow, gentle breezes of the Mandākinī, which were becoming cool with the water of perspiration;
its bright cheeks unstained by saffron, and its lovely ears beautiful even without ornaments? (37)
(Standing as if paralyzed, with compassion) Alas, indeed, O world!
Having reflected again and again for a long time, a beloved person, as if fashioned and placed before one's eyes, surely does not fail to provide comfort during exile.
Yet when the wife has passed away, the world becomes a withered wilderness, and thereafter, one is as if roasted upon a heap of chaff.

(Offstage) Vasiṣṭha, Vālmīki, the queens of Daśaratha, and Janaka, together with Arundhatī, having heard the quarrel of the children, are approaching with anxious minds; yet, their limbs overcome by old age and because the hermitage is so very distant, they move slowly, their matted locks hanging loose.
Rāma:

How is it that the venerable Arundhatī, Vasiṣṭha, my mothers, and Janaka are all right here? Indeed, how am I to see them? Now, the author of the commentary performs the auspicious rite (*maṅgalācāra*) upon the completion of the work: "Whatever I have performed throughout my life, whatever I shall perform hereafter out of passion, or even with the sense of duty as described in the various scriptures—all that is offered with faith at the pair of your lotus-feet, O Lord! O Kṛṣṇa!! There is no personal agency in me in this matter; for even that [agency] exists only through Your word."
Oṃ tat sat; may this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
